title: Certificates and Privileges
summary: What a private pilot may do, what must be in your pocket, and the endorsements that unlock bigger airplanes.
html:
Certificates, categories, classes

Your pilot certificate carries ratings. For airmen, a category is the broad group (airplane, rotorcraft, glider, lighter than air, powered lift). A class divides a category (single engine land, single engine sea, multiengine land, multiengine sea). A type rating is needed for large aircraft (over 12,500 pounds), turbojet powered airplanes, powered lift, and other aircraft the FAA specifies.

Documents you must have (61.3)

  • Pilot certificate
  • Government issued photo identification
  • Medical certificate, or a valid U.S. driver's license when flying under BasicMed

You must present your pilot certificate, medical, and photo ID on request to the FAA, an NTSB representative, a TSA representative, or any federal, state, or local law enforcement officer (61.3(l)), and your logbook on request to the FAA, the NTSB, or law enforcement (61.51(i)). You do not have to carry your logbook, except a student pilot on a solo cross country, who must carry the logbook with the required endorsements.

Private pilot privileges and limits (61.113)

The default rule: no acting as pilot in command for compensation or hire, and no carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire. The exceptions are what the test asks about.

ExceptionKey condition
Business incidentalFlight is only incidental to your business or job, and no passengers or property carried for hire
Cost sharingYou pay at least your pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees
Charitable or community eventMust meet 91.146: 500 hours, day VFR, nonstop, within 25 statute miles
Search and locationUnder a government or approved organization; you may be reimbursed fuel, oil, airport, and rental costs
Aircraft salesmanAt least 200 hours; may demonstrate to a prospective buyer
Glider or ultralight towingMeet 61.69

Cost sharing math: total qualifying cost divided by the number of occupants, including you. Four people and $320 means you pay at least $80.

Endorsements (61.31)

EndorsementApplies to
ComplexRetractable gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller (or FADEC)
High performanceEngine of more than 200 horsepower
High altitudePressurized aircraft with service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL
TailwheelAny tailwheel airplane; flight training plus a one time endorsement

Each is a one time endorsement from an authorized instructor after ground and flight training. None is a rating.

Student pilots

  • No passengers, no flights for compensation or hire, no business use
  • Solo visibility at least 3 statute miles by day, 5 statute miles at night
  • Must stay in visual reference to the surface
  • Need the appropriate solo and cross country endorsements

Recordkeeping

You must log only the time used for a certificate, rating, flight review, or recent experience. A private pilot logs pilot in command time when sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which the pilot is rated. Ratings, not endorsements, decide logging; endorsements decide whether you may act as pilot in command.

Address change and motor vehicle actions

  • New permanent mailing address: notify the FAA in writing; you may not exercise privileges after 30 days without doing so (61.60)
  • Alcohol or drug related motor vehicle action: written report to the FAA within 60 days (61.15)
keyFacts: Pilot certificate, photo ID, medical (or driver's license under BasicMed)
Retractable gear, flaps, controllable pitch propeller
Fuel, oil, airport expenditures, rental fees
Notify FAA; privileges stop after 30 days
memoryAids: Shareable costs are FOAR: Fuel, Oil, Airport expenditures, Rental fees.
High performance is MORE than 200; exactly 200 is not enough.
Ratings let you log it; endorsements let you act.
traps: Exactly 200 horsepower is not high performance.
Letting passengers pay the whole bill is compensation; you must pay at least your share.
Only a student on a solo cross country must carry the logbook.
The complex endorsement does not cover high performance, and the reverse is also true.
250 hours is the commercial minimum, not the charitable flight minimum of 500.

title: Currency and Flight Reviews
summary: Three numbers keep you legal: 24 calendar months, 90 days, and 1 hour after sunset.
html:
Flight review (61.56)

To act as pilot in command at all, solo or with passengers, you need a flight review within the preceding 24 calendar months. It is at least 1 hour of ground and 1 hour of flight training with an authorized instructor, covering the part 91 operating rules and the maneuvers the instructor chooses. It ends in a logbook endorsement, not a pass or fail grade.

These take its place:

  • A practical test for a new certificate, rating, or operating privilege (the 24 months restart from the test month)
  • A completed phase of an FAA pilot proficiency program such as WINGS

Calendar months run to the last day of the month. A review on June 14, 2024 is good through June 30, 2026.

Out of date? You may still fly with an instructor, who can give you the review. You may not fly solo.

Passenger currency (61.57)

SituationRequirement within preceding 90 days
Day passengers3 takeoffs and 3 landings, sole manipulator, same category and class (and type if required)
Tailwheel passengers3 landings to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane
Night passengers3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop, from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise, same category and class

Make and model do not matter: landings in a Cessna 172 count for a Piper Cherokee because both are airplane single engine land. If you are out of currency, make the landings solo or with an instructor before any passenger boards.

Three different nights

PeriodUsed for
Sunset to sunrisePosition lights required (91.209)
End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilightDefinition of night (Part 1): logging night time and night equipment
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunriseNight passenger currency landings (61.57(b))

Currency is not proficiency

Meeting 61.57 means you are legal, not that you are ready for a gusty crosswind at an unfamiliar field. Build personal minimums that tighten when you have not flown recently, and fly with an instructor when the conditions exceed your recent experience.
keyFacts: 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days, same category and class
3 full stop landings in a tailwheel airplane
3 full stop landings, 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight
memoryAids: Review every 24, land 3 in 90.
Night has three clocks: lights at sunset, logging at twilight, landings an hour after sunset.
traps: Using the exact anniversary date instead of the end of the month.
Counting landings made after sunset but before 1 hour after sunset toward night currency.
Thinking you can fly solo without a current flight review.
Thinking make and model must match for passenger currency.
Restarting the 24 months from the old due date instead of the practical test month.

title: Medicals and BasicMed
summary: How long your medical lasts, when BasicMed works instead, and when you must ground yourself.
html:
Medical certificate durations (61.23)

Duration depends on your age on the exam date and the privileges you use. Every period ends on the last day of the month.

Privileges usedUnder 40 at exam40 or older at exam
Airline transport pilot (first class)12 months6 months
Commercial pilot (first or second class)12 months12 months
Private, recreational, student (any class)60 months24 months

A first class medical that lapses for airline privileges keeps working at the lower levels until those periods end. Turning 40 after the exam does not shorten anything.

Self grounding (61.53)

Even with a valid medical, you may not act as pilot in command while you know of a medical condition, or are taking medication or treatment, that would make you unable to meet the standards for your medical. Under BasicMed the test in 61.53(b) and (c) is slightly different: you may not act as pilot in command while you know of any medical condition that would make you unable to operate the aircraft safely.

BasicMed (61.23(c)(3), 61.113(i), part 68)

Eligibility

  • Valid U.S. driver's license, and comply with its restrictions
  • Held an FAA medical certificate at any time after July 14, 2006
  • Most recent medical not suspended or revoked, most recent special issuance not withdrawn, most recent application not denied
  • Medical education course within the preceding 24 calendar months
  • Comprehensive exam by a state licensed physician within the preceding 48 calendar months

Operating limits

ItemLimit
Aircraft occupantsAuthorized to carry no more than 7
Passengers aboardNo more than 6
Maximum takeoff weight12,500 pounds or less
AltitudeNot above 18,000 feet MSL
SpeedNot above 250 knots indicated
LocationWithin the United States unless the other country allows it

Night and IFR are allowed if you are otherwise rated and current. The signed exam checklist and the course certificate are kept with your logbook. In the airplane you carry the driver's license in place of a medical certificate.

Alcohol and drug reporting

An alcohol or drug related motor vehicle action (conviction, or license suspension, revocation, or denial) must be reported in writing to the FAA within 60 days. Two within 3 years is grounds to deny, suspend, or revoke a certificate.
memoryAids: BasicMed exam 48, course 24: the exam is the bigger number.
Under 40 gets 60; 40 and up gets 24 for private.
traps: Using today's age instead of age at the exam date.
Swapping the 24 month course and the 48 month exam.
Thinking BasicMed bans night or IFR flight.
Thinking a valid medical overrides 61.53 when you are taking a disqualifying medication.
Thinking a pilot who never held a medical can start on BasicMed.

title: Airworthiness and Inspections
summary: The papers on board, the inspections in the logbooks, and who is on the hook for each.
html:
Documents on board: ARROW

LetterDocumentNote
AAirworthiness certificateDisplayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance, legible to passengers or crew
RRegistration certificateRequired on board
RRadio station licenseOnly for flights outside the United States
OOperating limitationsFlight manual, placards, and markings
WWeight and balanceCurrent data for the airplane

Maintenance records do not need to be on board.

Who is responsible

  • Owner or operator: primarily responsible for keeping the aircraft airworthy, including ADs (91.403)
  • Pilot in command: decides whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight, and must end the flight if an unairworthy condition occurs (91.7)

Inspections

ItemIntervalRule
Annual inspection12 calendar months91.409(a)
100 hour inspection (carrying people for hire, or instruction for hire in an airplane the instructor provides)100 hours time in service91.409(b)
Transponder24 calendar months91.413
Altimeter and static system (IFR in controlled airspace only)24 calendar months91.411
ELT12 calendar months91.207(d)

The 100 hour rules

  • An annual counts as a 100 hour; a 100 hour counts as an annual only if an IA does it and records it as an annual
  • You may run up to 10 hours over, only to get to a place where the inspection can be done
  • The overrun is subtracted from the next interval: due at 1,450, done at 1,456, next due at 1,550

Who signs

  • Annual: an A&P mechanic with an Inspection Authorization (or a repair station or manufacturer)
  • 100 hour: an A&P mechanic is enough

Airworthiness directives

An AD is a mandatory rule that fixes an unsafe condition. It applies to every operation, private or for hire. The records must show the current status of each applicable AD, the method of compliance, and for a recurring AD, when the next action is due. A Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin is advisory only.

Special flight permit

An airplane that does not meet airworthiness requirements but can still fly safely may be issued a special flight permit, for example to ferry it to a maintenance base, to evacuate it from danger, or when the annual is out of date. Apply to the FAA Flight Standards District Office.

Preventive maintenance

A certificated pilot may do the preventive maintenance items in part 43 Appendix A on an aircraft the pilot owns or operates, when it is not used under part 121, 129, or 135. Examples: removing, installing, and repairing landing gear tires; cleaning and greasing wheel bearings; replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap; cleaning or replacing fuel and oil strainers or filter elements; replacing bulbs, reflectors, and lenses of position and landing lights; replacing and servicing batteries; replacing safety belts. Record the work with a description, the date, your name, signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate.
keyFacts: Airworthiness, Registration, Radio license, Operating limits, Weight and balance
For hire operations; 10 hour overrun only to reach inspection
memoryAids: ARROW for paperwork in the airplane, and the radio license only goes abroad.
Annual by IA, hundred by any A and P mechanic.
traps: Applying the 10 hour overrun to an annual.
Counting the next 100 hour from when it was actually done instead of when it was due.
Thinking the PIC, not the owner, is primarily responsible for AD compliance.
Thinking an annual does not reset the 100 hour clock.
Using the exact date rather than the end of the month for calendar month items.

title: Required and Inoperative Equipment
summary: What must work for day and night VFR, how to decide on a broken item, and the ELT, transponder, and ADS-B rules.
html:
Day VFR equipment (91.205(b))

Two popular memory aids, ATOMATOFLAMES and A TOMATO FLAMES, both list:

  • Airspeed indicator, Tachometer, Oil pressure gauge, Manifold pressure gauge (altitude engine), Altimeter, Temperature gauge (liquid cooled), Oil temperature gauge (air cooled), Fuel gauge for each tank
  • Landing gear position indicator (retractable), Anticollision lights (airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996), Magnetic compass, ELT if required, Safety belts (each occupant 2 or older) and shoulder harnesses (front seats in small airplanes built after July 18, 1978, all seats after December 12, 1986)
  • Not in the acronym: flotation gear and a pyrotechnic signal device if operated for hire over water beyond power off gliding distance from shore

Night VFR adds (91.205(c)): FLAPS

  • Fuses: one spare set, or three of each kind, accessible in flight
  • Landing light: only if operated for hire
  • Anticollision lights
  • Position lights
  • Source of electricity adequate for all installed equipment

Flying with inoperative equipment (91.213(d))

For a small airplane with no MEL, ask four questions. If the answer to any is yes, the item must be fixed (or a special flight permit obtained).

  1. Is it part of the VFR day type certification equipment?
  2. Is it required by the equipment list or the KOEL for this kind of operation?
  3. Is it required by 91.205 or any other rule for this kind of operation?
  4. Is it required by an AD?

If all four are no, the item must be removed (cockpit control placarded, maintenance recorded) or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative", and a pilot or mechanic must decide it is not a hazard.

MEL and KOEL

  • MEL: approved for a specific airplane. The MEL plus the FAA letter of authorization count as a supplemental type certificate; the letter must be on board.
  • KOEL: in the flight manual, lists equipment required for day VFR, night VFR, IFR, or known icing. It does not authorize deferrals.

ELT (91.207)

ItemRule
InspectionWithin 12 calendar months
Battery replacementAfter more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or 50 percent of useful life
Removed for repairFly up to 90 days, logged, placard "ELT not installed"
ExemptTraining within 50 NM of the departure airport, aircraft for one person, and a few others

Transponder and ADS-B Out (91.215, 91.225)

Mode C and ADS-B Out are required in:

  • Class A, B, and C airspace
  • Within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport, surface to 10,000 feet MSL (the Mode C veil)
  • Above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of Class B or C, up to 10,000 feet MSL
  • Class E at and above 10,000 feet MSL in the 48 states, excluding at and below 2,500 feet AGL

Aircraft not originally certificated with an engine driven electrical system, balloons, and gliders have limited exceptions, mainly within the Mode C veil while staying outside Class B and C airspace.

The transponder must have been tested within 24 calendar months (91.413) for any use, VFR or IFR. The altimeter and static check of 91.411 is for IFR only.

Type cert, equipment list or KOEL, 91.205 or other rule, AD
Requires FAA letter of authorization on board
1 cumulative hour or 50 percent of life
30 NM of Class B primary, surface to 10,000 MSL
memoryAids: A TOMATO FLAMES for day; add FLAPS for night.
Inoperative item: TERA (Type certificate, Equipment list or KOEL, Rule, AD). Any yes means no go.
traps: Thinking a landing light is required for every night flight.
Applying the 91.411 IFR test to a VFR only flight.
Thinking a visual fuel check makes an inoperative fuel gauge acceptable.
Forgetting to placard a deferred item.
Forgetting the 2,500 feet AGL exclusion for ADS-B and transponder above 10,000 MSL.

title: Part 91 Operating Rules
summary: The rules that govern every flight: authority, alcohol, preflight, right of way, speed, altitude, fuel, oxygen, and aerobatics.
html:
Authority and responsibility

  • 91.3: the pilot in command is the final authority. In an emergency you may deviate from any part 91 rule as needed, and send a written report only if the FAA asks.
  • 91.7: you decide whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight; stop the flight when an unairworthy condition occurs.
  • 91.13: no careless or reckless operation that endangers life or property.
  • 91.15: you may drop objects if you take reasonable precautions against injury or damage.

Alcohol and drugs (91.17)

No flying within 8 hours of drinking alcohol, while under the influence, or with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or more. All three must be satisfied. No carrying a person who appears intoxicated, except in an emergency or a medical patient under proper care.

Preflight action (91.103)

For every flight: runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data. For flights away from the airport vicinity, add weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, and known traffic delays.

Belts and passengers (91.105, 91.107)

  • Brief each passenger on how to fasten and unfasten belts and harness, and tell them to fasten them
  • Everyone belted during taxi, takeoff, and landing; a child under 2 may be held by an adult in an approved seat
  • Required crew keep belts fastened at their stations, and shoulder harnesses during takeoff and landing

Right of way (91.113)

  • Aircraft in distress first
  • Balloon, then glider, then airship, then airplane and rotorcraft (the less maneuverable has priority)
  • An aircraft towing or refueling others has priority over all other powered aircraft
  • Converging, same category: the aircraft on the right has the right of way
  • Head on: both turn right
  • Overtaking: the one being overtaken has the right of way; pass well clear on the right
  • Landing: the lower aircraft has the right of way, but may not cut in front of another

Speed limits (91.117)

WhereMax indicated
Below 10,000 feet MSL250 knots
At or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport200 knots
Under a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor200 knots

Minimum altitudes (91.119)

AreaMinimum
AnywhereHigh enough for an emergency landing without undue hazard
Congested area1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally
Other than congested500 feet above the surface
Open water or sparsely populatedNo closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure

Altimeter, fuel, altitudes

  • Altimeter (91.121): below 18,000 MSL, use a station along the route within 100 NM; no radio, use field elevation
  • VFR fuel (91.151): to the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes by day, 45 minutes by night, at normal cruise
  • VFR cruise (91.159): above 3,000 feet AGL, by magnetic course; 0 to 179 degrees odd thousand plus 500, 180 to 359 degrees even thousand plus 500

Oxygen (91.211)

Cabin pressure altitudeRequirement
Above 12,500 up to 14,000 feet MSLRequired crew use oxygen for time beyond 30 minutes
Above 14,000 feet MSLRequired crew use oxygen the entire time
Above 15,000 feet MSLEach occupant must be provided oxygen

Formation, aerobatics, parachutes, experimental

  • Formation (91.111): only by arrangement with each pilot in command; never with passengers for hire
  • Aerobatics (91.303): not over congested areas or open air assemblies, not in surface area Class B, C, D, or E, not within 4 NM of a federal airway centerline, not below 1,500 feet AGL, not with visibility under 3 SM
  • Parachutes (91.307): with anyone aboard besides crew, a maneuver beyond 60 degrees bank or 30 degrees pitch requires every occupant to wear one; synthetic packed within 180 days, natural fiber within 60 days
  • Experimental (91.319): no carrying people or property for hire in operations that need an air carrier or commercial operator certificate, tell each passenger it is experimental, day VFR only and no densely populated areas unless authorized

Class D entry (91.129)

Two way radio communication must be established before entering. If the controller answers with your call sign, even saying "stand by," you are established. "Aircraft calling, stand by" means stay out.

title: Accidents and NTSB Part 830
summary: What counts as an accident, what you must report right away, and what you may touch afterward.
html:
Definitions (830.2)

An aircraft accident is an occurrence associated with operating an aircraft, between boarding with intent of flight and when all persons have left the aircraft, in which anyone suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage.

Serious injury

  • Hospitalization for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days of the injury
  • Any fracture, except simple fractures of fingers, toes, or nose
  • Severe hemorrhage, or nerve, muscle, or tendon damage
  • Injury to an internal organ
  • Second or third degree burns, or any burns over more than 5 percent of the body

Substantial damage

Damage or failure that adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair or replacement. It does not include: engine failure or damage limited to one engine, bent fairings or cowling, dented skin, small punctured holes in skin or fabric, ground damage to propeller blades, or damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes, or wingtips.

Immediate notification (830.5)

Notify the nearest NTSB office immediately for any accident, an overdue aircraft believed to be in an accident, or any of these serious incidents, among others:

  • Flight control system malfunction or failure
  • A required crewmember unable to perform normal duties because of injury or illness
  • In flight fire
  • Aircraft collision in flight
  • Damage to property other than the aircraft estimated over $25,000
  • Release of all or part of a propeller blade, other than by ground contact
  • Turbine engine failure with debris released other than out the exhaust

Wreckage and records (830.10)

Do not disturb wreckage until the NTSB takes custody, except to remove injured or trapped persons, protect the wreckage from further damage, or protect the public from injury. If you must move it, sketch, note, and photograph its original position if you can. Keep all records related to the event.

Written reports (830.15)

EventWritten report
AccidentWithin 10 days
Overdue aircraft still missingAfter 7 days
Serious incidentOnly if the NTSB requests it
keyFacts: Death, serious injury, or substantial damage
More than 48 hours, starting within 7 days
Gear, wheels, tires, flaps, brakes, wingtips, dented skin
Rescue people, protect wreckage, protect public
memoryAids: Ten days for the crash, seven days if still lost.
Incidents to call about: controls, crew, fire, collision, property, prop blade.
traps: Calling a ground loop with only gear and wingtip damage an accident.
Confusing the $25,000 property damage item with aircraft damage.
Thinking any overnight hospital stay is a serious injury.
Thinking a reportable incident always needs a written report.
Moving wreckage to clear a runway before the NTSB releases it.

title: The Airspace Classes
summary: Six letters describe every piece of sky over the United States; learn their shapes and what each one means for you.
html:
Controlled versus uncontrolled

Controlled airspace (Classes A, B, C, D, E) is airspace where ATC provides service to IFR flights. It does not mean a VFR pilot is always talking to ATC. Uncontrolled airspace is Class G. The class decides three things for you: what you must do to enter, what equipment you need, and which VFR weather minimums apply.

The classes at a glance

ClassTypical shapeChart symbol
A18,000 MSL up to and including FL600Not shown on sectionals
BSurface to about 10,000 MSL, upside down wedding cake around the busiest airportsSolid blue lines, altitudes in hundreds of feet MSL
C5 NM core from the surface, 10 NM shelf from about 1,200 AGL, top about 4,000 above the airportSolid magenta lines
DSurface to about 2,500 above the airport, radius tailored to the airportDashed blue line, ceiling in a dashed box in MSL
EEverything controlled that is not A, B, C, or DMagenta vignette (700 AGL floor), blue vignette (1,200 AGL or higher), dashed magenta (surface)
GBelow the Class E floorImplied by the Class E floor around it

Class A

From 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600. IFR only, so no private pilot without an instrument rating ever flies VFR there. Altimeters are set to 29.92.

Class B

Surrounds the busiest airports. Each shelf is charted as ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet MSL, for example 100 over 40 means 4,000 to 10,000 feet MSL. You need a clearance to enter.

Class C

A standard Class C has a 5 NM surface area and a 10 NM shelf beginning about 1,200 feet above the airport, both topping out about 4,000 feet above the airport. Beyond that lies an outer area, normally 20 NM, where approach control offers service but participation is not required.

Class D

Airports with an operating tower but not busy enough for B or C. Usually surface to about 2,500 feet above the field. A ceiling in brackets such as [25] is MSL. A minus value such as [-25] means up to but not including that altitude, because another class begins there. When a part time tower closes, the surface area normally becomes Class E if weather reporting continues, or Class G if it does not; the Chart Supplement says which.

Class E

The gap filler. It starts at the surface around some nontowered airports (dashed magenta), at 700 feet AGL inside a magenta vignette, at 1,200 feet AGL inside a blue vignette or along Victor airways, and everywhere at 14,500 feet MSL. It continues up to, but not into, Class A at 18,000 feet MSL. It also starts again above FL600.

Class G

Whatever lies below the Class E floor. Over most of the country that is the surface to 700 or 1,200 feet AGL. In some remote mountain areas Class G extends up to 14,500 feet MSL.

How to think about it

Picture a layer cake: Class G at the bottom, Class E as the big middle, Class A on top, with B, C, and D drilled in around busy airports. At any point ask two questions: what is the floor of the controlled airspace here, and is there a B, C, or D cylinder around me at this altitude?

5 NM surface area, 10 NM shelf from about 1,200 above the airport
About 2,500 above the airport, charted MSL
Up to but not including the charted value
Class E from 1,200 AGL to but not including 18,000 MSL, 4 NM each side
Class D becomes E with weather reporting, otherwise G
memoryAids: A is Above (18,000), B is Busiest, C is Commercial, D is Dinky, E is Everywhere else, G is Ground level.
Class C numbers: 5, 10, 20 NM and 1,200 and 4,000 feet.
traps: Thinking controlled airspace means you must talk to ATC. Class E is controlled and needs no contact.
Reading Class B, C, or D altitudes as AGL. Every charted airspace altitude in a box or stack is MSL.
Assuming a closed tower means Class G. With weather reporting it is normally Class E.
Forgetting that Class E begins at 14,500 MSL everywhere, even where no vignette is charted.

title: VFR Weather Minimums
summary: One table from 91.155 drives a big share of the knowledge test; learn it cold, then learn the exceptions.
html:
The table (14 CFR 91.155)

AirspaceFlight visibilityCloud clearance
Class ANot applicableNot applicable (IFR only)
Class B3 SMClear of clouds
Class C3 SM500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
Class D3 SM500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
Class E below 10,000 MSL3 SM500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
Class E at or above 10,000 MSL5 SM1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal
Class G, 1,200 AGL or less, day1 SMClear of clouds
Class G, 1,200 AGL or less, night3 SM500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
Class G, above 1,200 AGL but below 10,000 MSL, day1 SM500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
Class G, above 1,200 AGL but below 10,000 MSL, night3 SM500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
Class G, above 1,200 AGL and at or above 10,000 MSL5 SM1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal

Reading the table correctly

  • Class G rows depend on height above the surface, not MSL. Over a 9,800 foot plateau at 10,500 MSL you are only 700 AGL, so the low Class G row applies.
  • Class B is the odd one: 3 SM and clear of clouds, because ATC separates everyone.
  • The 10,000 foot MSL line is where speeds get higher, so visibility goes to 5 SM and clearances to 1,000, 1,000, 1 SM.

The Class G night exception

At night in Class G below 1,200 AGL you may fly with 1 SM and clear of clouds only in an airport traffic pattern within one half mile of the runway.

Surface area rules (91.155(c) and (d))

Within the lateral boundaries of a Class B, C, D, or E surface area, without special VFR:

  • No VFR beneath the ceiling when the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet.
  • No takeoff, landing, or entering the traffic pattern unless ground visibility is at least 3 SM, or flight visibility is at least 3 SM when ground visibility is not reported.

This applies at a nontowered airport inside a dashed magenta Class E surface area too.

Special VFR (91.157)

Times of use, altitudes, and controlling agencies for SUA are printed on the sectional margin. A note such as "excludes airspace 1,500 AGL and below" lowers or raises the effective boundary.

Military training routes

  • IR routes are flown under IFR, VR routes under VFR, regardless of weather.
  • Four digit numbers: entirely at or below 1,500 AGL. Three digits or fewer: at least one segment above 1,500 AGL.
  • Speeds often exceed 250 knots. Check activity with Flight Service and look hard when crossing the gray lines.

Temporary flight restrictions

Issued by NOTAM, often on short notice, so a printed chart cannot show the ones in effect for your flight. Common types: disaster and hazard areas such as wildfires (91.137), presidential and VIP movement (91.141), space operations (91.143), and aerial demonstrations and major sporting events (91.145). A thorough briefing is the defense.

ADIZ, SFRA, and SATR

  • ADIZ: an identification zone at the national boundary. Flight plan before entering, two way radio, Mode C transponder.
  • Washington DC SFRA: 30 NM from DCA with a flight restricted zone near the center. Special awareness training is required to fly VFR within 60 NM of DCA.
  • Special air traffic rule areas under Part 93, such as south of Luke AFB: the chart box spells out the requirement, typically two way communication with a named facility.

Other airspace areas

  • Wildlife refuges, national parks, wilderness areas: pilots are requested to fly at least 2,000 feet above the surface.
  • TRSA: radar service around some Class D airports, VFR participation voluntary.
  • Parachute jumping areas, glider, ultralight, and hang glider activity: magenta symbols, details in the Chart Supplement.
  • Local airport advisory areas, VFR flyways, and terminal area chart notes help with routing near Class B.

Risk management on the route

Legal entry into an active MOA or across an MTR is not the same as a safe plan. Ask Flight Service about activity, use flight following, and route around when military aircraft are working the area.

title: Reading the Sectional
summary: Airport data blocks, obstruction labels, and the MEF tell you most of what you need to plan a safe altitude.
html:
Airport symbols and colors

  • Blue airport: control tower. Magenta airport: no tower.
  • Circle with runway pattern drawn inside: hard surfaced runways 1,500 to 8,069 feet. Runway outline alone: longer than 8,069 feet.
  • Open circle: soft surface or short runway. R in a circle: restricted or private, use only in an emergency or with specific permission.
  • Small ticks around the symbol: fuel and services available. Star on top: rotating beacon sunset to sunrise.

The data block

ItemExampleMeaning
TowerCT 118.1 with a starTower frequency; star means part time
WeatherATIS 119.65, ASOS 118.725, AWOS 3Recorded or automated weather frequency

Obstructions

  • Label 549 (428): top 549 MSL, height 428 AGL. Never add them.
  • Small inverted V: below 1,000 AGL. Taller symbol: 1,000 AGL and higher. Two symbols joined: group obstruction.
  • Lightning marks: high intensity lights. UC: under construction or reported, not verified.

Maximum elevation figure

The large blue number in each quadrant, such as 11 with a superscript 7, is 11,700 feet MSL. It covers the highest known terrain or obstacle in that quadrant, rounded up with a buffer. It is not the exact terrain height and not an IFR minimum altitude.

Choosing an altitude

  • Start at the MEF of each quadrant on the route, add your margin, and then fit the VFR cruising altitude rule (odd thousands plus 500 eastbound, even thousands plus 500 westbound) above 3,000 AGL.
  • For a pattern altitude, add the pattern height to field elevation: a 1,716 foot field with a 1,000 foot pattern means about 2,700 MSL.
  • Higher altitude buys glide distance and terrain clearance, but check winds aloft and airspace floors.

Latitude and longitude

Parallels and meridians are drawn every 30 minutes with one minute ticks. Find the labeled lines nearest the point, count ticks, and remember latitude grows northward and west longitude grows westward.

Navaids and frequencies

  • Blue boxes: VOR, VORTAC, VOR/DME with frequency and identifier. Magenta boxes: NDB, frequency in kHz.
  • A box such as CTC NORCAL APP WITHIN 20 NM ON 125.35 gives the approach frequency for that sector.
  • Heavy line FSS box: Flight Service frequencies; R after a frequency means receive only.

A four step method

  1. Is the point inside a B, C, or D boundary? Read its ceiling over floor numbers.
  2. Is the altitude between that floor and ceiling? If yes, you are in that class.
  3. If not, find the Class E floor: dashed magenta means surface, magenta vignette means 700 AGL, blue vignette or open country means 1,200 AGL, and everywhere Class E starts by 14,500 MSL.
  4. Below the Class E floor you are in Class G. At and above 18,000 MSL you are in Class A.

title: Atmosphere, Pressure and Density Altitude
summary: Know the standard atmosphere cold, and you can predict what nonstandard pressure and temperature will do to your altimeter and your takeoff roll.
html:
What the air is made of

Dry air is about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen and 1 percent other gases (mostly argon, plus carbon dioxide). Water vapor varies from almost zero to a few percent, but it drives nearly all weather. Most weather happens in the troposphere, the lowest layer, where temperature normally decreases with height. Its top, the tropopause, is roughly 36,000 feet in the middle latitudes.

The standard atmosphere

ItemStandard value
Sea level temperature15 degrees C (59 degrees F)
Sea level pressure29.92 inches Hg (1013.2 hPa)
Temperature lapse rateAbout 2 degrees C (3.5 degrees F) per 1,000 feet
Pressure lapse rate (low altitude)About 1 inch Hg per 1,000 feet

Standard temperature at any altitude: 15 minus 2 per thousand feet. At 5,000 feet it is 5 degrees C; at 6,000 feet it is 3 degrees C (about 37 degrees F).

Pressure and the altimeter

Your altimeter is a barometer. Fly from high pressure toward low pressure without resetting it and it reads too high: the airplane is lower than the needle says. Each 0.01 inch of error is about 10 feet. Example: set to 30.12, actual 29.82, error 0.30 inch, so indicated 5,500 feet is really about 5,200 feet.

Temperature works the same way. Cold air is dense, the pressure levels squeeze together, and the altimeter overreads. The altimeter setting fixes pressure error only; it does not correct for temperature.

High to low, or hot to cold: look out below.

Density altitude

Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. It is the altitude the airplane and engine actually feel. Three weather factors raise it:

  • Higher temperature (the biggest factor day to day)
  • Lower pressure (high elevation or a low pressure system)
  • Higher humidity (water vapor is lighter than the dry air it displaces)

High density altitude means less lift, less engine power and less propeller thrust: longer takeoff roll, lower climb rate, higher true airspeed on approach for the same indicated airspeed, and longer landing roll.

Using the Figure 8 chart

  1. Find pressure altitude: field elevation plus the conversion factor beside the altimeter setting (positive below 29.92, negative above).
  2. Enter the bottom scale at the outside air temperature and go straight up to the pressure altitude line.
  3. Read across to the left scale for density altitude.

Rule of thumb check: density altitude rises about 120 feet for every 1 degree C above standard temperature.

Elevation 4,702, altimeter 29.60 (plus 298), 95 degrees FPressure altitude 5,000; density altitude about 8,200
Pressure altitude 6,000, 90 degrees FDensity altitude about 9,100

title: Stability, Lapse Rates and Inversions
summary: Stability decides whether the sky gives you smooth stratus and haze or bumpy cumulus and storms.
html:
The core idea

Lift a small parcel of air. It expands and cools. If it ends up colder than the air around it, it sinks back: the air is stable. If it stays warmer, it keeps rising: the air is unstable. Stability is a comparison between the parcel's cooling rate and the actual lapse rate of the surrounding air.

Three lapse rates you must not mix up

NameRate per 1,000 feetWhat it describes
Standard lapse rate2 degrees C (3.5 F)The average atmosphere, for reference
Dry adiabatic3 degrees C (5.4 F)A rising unsaturated parcel
Moist adiabaticAbout 1.1 to 2.8 degrees CA rising saturated parcel, slowed by latent heat of condensation
  • Environment cools faster than the parcel: unstable.
  • Environment cools slower than the parcel: stable.
  • Between the moist and dry rates: conditionally unstable (stable until saturated, unstable once a cloud forms).

What makes air less stable: heating from below and adding moisture at low levels, or cooling aloft. What makes it more stable: cooling from below or warming aloft.

Stable versus unstable air

Stable airUnstable air
Stratiform cloudsCumuliform clouds
Continuous precipitationShowery precipitation
Smooth airTurbulence
Fair to poor visibility (haze, smoke, fog)Good visibility outside showers

Temperature inversions

An inversion is a layer where temperature increases with height. It is extremely stable.

  • Surface inversion: forms on clear, calm nights as the ground radiates heat away. Expect haze, smoke, fog and poor visibility below, often a crisp haze top, warmer air and better visibility above.
  • Inversion aloft: from sinking air in a high or along a frontal surface. Flat cumulus tops at one level often mark it.
  • Wind shear: a calm surface layer under strong wind just above can create shear when climbing or descending through the inversion top.

Using a briefing to find the lapse rate

Take two temperatures from the winds aloft, divide the difference by the thousands of feet between them. In Figure 13, 20 degrees C at 3,000 feet and 8 degrees C at 9,000 feet give 12 over 6, or 2 degrees C per 1,000 feet.

About 1.1 to 2.8 degrees C per 1,000 feet
Environment cools faster than a lifted parcel
Stratiform clouds, steady precipitation, smooth air, poor visibility
Cumuliform clouds, showers, turbulence, good visibility
Temperature increases with altitude; very stable
Radiational cooling on clear, calm nights
memoryAids: Stable is stratus, steady, smooth and smoky.
Warm parcel rises, cold parcel sinks.
traps: Confusing the standard lapse rate (2 C) with the dry adiabatic rate (3 C).
Thinking an inversion means colder air above. It means warmer air above.
Expecting good visibility under an inversion; pollutants are trapped there.
Assuming flat cumulus tops mark the freezing level rather than a stable layer.

title: Wind, Wind Shear, Mountain Wave and Turbulence
summary: Pressure differences start the wind, Earth's rotation bends it, and terrain, fronts and storms make it dangerous.
html:
Why the wind blows

  • Pressure gradient force pushes air from high toward low pressure. Tight isobars mean strong wind.
  • Coriolis force deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. Result: clockwise flow out of a high, counterclockwise flow into a low.
  • Friction slows the wind within roughly 2,000 feet of the ground. Slower wind means weaker Coriolis, so surface wind cuts across the isobars toward low pressure and is backed (more counterclockwise) compared with the wind aloft.

Aloft, pressure gradient and Coriolis balance and the wind flows parallel to the isobars. That is why a surface wind from the south often becomes southwest at a few thousand feet.

Local winds

WindWhenDirection
Sea or lake breezeDayWater toward land (land heats faster)
Land breezeNightLand toward water (land cools faster)
Valley windDayUpslope, warmed air rises along the slopes
Mountain windNightDownslope, cool dense air drains into the valley

Mountain wave and rotor

Ingredients: strong wind blowing nearly perpendicular to the ridge and a stable layer near the ridge top. Air oscillates downstream for many miles.

  • Lenticular clouds: smooth, lens shaped, stationary in the wave crests. They look calm but mark strong vertical currents.
  • Rotor: a rolling eddy below the crests on the lee side, sometimes shown by a ragged roll cloud. Often the worst turbulence in the system, severe or extreme near ridge level.
  • Lee side downdrafts can exceed a light airplane's climb rate. Cross ridges with plenty of altitude, at an angle that allows a quick turn away, or do not cross at all.

Wind shear

A sudden change in wind speed or direction, or both, over a short distance, at any altitude. Sources: thunderstorms and microbursts, fronts, temperature inversions, terrain and the jet stream.

  • Inversion shear: calm surface air under a wind of 25 knots or more a few thousand feet up. Expect a jolt as you climb or descend through the inversion top.
  • Losing headwind or gaining tailwind: indicated airspeed drops and the airplane sinks. Add power and pitch promptly.
  • Gaining headwind: airspeed jumps and the airplane balloons. Near a storm, this can be the first half of a microburst.

Turbulence types

TypeCauseWhere
MechanicalWind over buildings, trees, terrainLow level, downwind of obstructions
Convective (thermal)Uneven surface heatingBelow cumulus bases on hot afternoons
FrontalLifting of warm air at a frontAlong fast moving cold fronts
WakeWingtip vorticesBehind and below heavy, slow, clean airplanes
Clear airShear, often near the jet streamHigh altitude, no visual cue

In turbulence, slow to or below maneuvering speed for your weight, hold attitude and accept altitude excursions.

traps: Thinking wind shear only happens in thunderstorms.

title: Moisture, Clouds and Precipitation
summary: Temperature and dewpoint tell you where clouds will form, how high the bases are, and when fog is coming.
html:
Moisture vocabulary

  • Dewpoint: the temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated. It measures the actual moisture in the air.
  • Relative humidity: moisture present compared with what the air could hold at its current temperature. Cool the air and relative humidity rises even though moisture is unchanged.
  • Spread: temperature minus dewpoint. A small spread (about 3 degrees C or 5 degrees F or less) and shrinking means fog or low clouds are likely.

Water changes state by evaporation, condensation, freezing, melting, sublimation (solid to vapor) and deposition (vapor to solid). Condensation and freezing release heat; evaporation and melting absorb it.

Estimating cumulus cloud bases

Rising air and its dewpoint converge at about 4.4 degrees F or 2.5 degrees C per 1,000 feet.

UnitsFormula
FahrenheitSpread divided by 4.4, times 1,000 = base in feet AGL
CelsiusSpread divided by 2.5, times 1,000 = base in feet AGL

Examples: 82 F and 60 F give a 22 F spread, bases about 5,000 feet AGL; add field elevation for MSL. A METAR with 25/17 gives an 8 C spread, bases about 3,200 feet AGL.

How air is lifted to form clouds

  1. Convection: surface heating
  2. Orographic: wind forced up terrain
  3. Frontal: warm air pushed up over cold air
  4. Convergence: air piling together and rising

Stable air lifted makes stratiform clouds; unstable air lifted makes cumuliform clouds.

Cloud families

FamilyTypical basesExamples
LowSurface to about 6,500 feet AGLStratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus
MiddleAbout 6,500 to 20,000 feet AGLAltostratus, altocumulus
HighAbove about 20,000 feet AGLCirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus (ice crystals)
Vertical developmentLow bases, tops can exceed 50,000 feetTowering cumulus, cumulonimbus

Name clues: nimbo or nimbus means rain bearing; alto means middle; cirro means high; castellanus means turret shaped, a sign of midlevel instability and possible afternoon storms. Lenticular clouds mean mountain wave.

Precipitation clues

  • Steady precipitation: stable air, stratiform clouds. Showers: unstable air, cumuliform clouds.
  • Precipitation generally needs clouds about 4,000 feet thick or more to fall.
  • Ice pellets at the surface mean freezing rain is falling at a higher altitude, so a warm layer exists aloft.
  • Freezing rain is liquid rain that freezes on contact with surfaces below 0 degrees C; it builds clear ice fast.
  • Virga is precipitation that evaporates before reaching the ground. Evaporative cooling can drive strong downdrafts and dry microbursts beneath it.

Spread divided by 2.5 = thousands of feet AGL

title: Air Masses and Fronts
summary: Every front brings a wind shift; the type of front and the stability of the air decide what else comes with it.
html:
Air masses

An air mass is a large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and moisture, taken on from its source region. It changes as it moves.

  • Cold air over a warm surface: heated from below, becomes unstable. Cumulus, turbulence, showers, good visibility.
  • Warm air over a cold surface: cooled from below, becomes stable. Stratus, fog, haze, smooth air, poor visibility.

What every front brings

A front is the boundary between air masses of different density. Crossing any front, even a dry one with no clouds, you can expect a wind shift plus changes in temperature, dewpoint and pressure. The wind shift is the most reliable sign.

Front by front

FrontHow it formsTypical weather
ColdCold air pushes under warm air; steep slope, faster movingNarrow band of cumuliform clouds, showers, possible thunderstorms and squall lines ahead; gusty wind, turbulence; rapid clearing, cooler and drier behind
WarmWarm air rides up over cold air; gentle slope, slowerCirrus far ahead, then cirrostratus, altostratus, nimbostratus; wide area of steady precipitation, low ceilings, fog; embedded thunderstorms if the warm air is unstable
StationaryNeither air mass advancingWeather similar to a warm front that can linger for days
OccludedFast cold front overtakes a warm front, lifting warm air aloftMix of cold and warm front weather; possible embedded thunderstorms

The cold front wind shift

In the Northern Hemisphere the wind ahead of a cold front is usually south or southwest. After passage it shifts to west or northwest. Pressure falls as the front approaches, is lowest at the front, and rises after it passes. Temperature and dewpoint drop behind it.

Stability decides the weather

Air being liftedResult
Moist and stableStratiform clouds, steady precipitation
Moist and unstableCumuliform clouds, showers, thunderstorms
DryFew or no clouds, but still a wind shift

Stable: stratus, fog, haze, smooth air

Narrow band of cumulus and storms, then rapid clearing

Cirrus first means a warm front is coming.

title: Thunderstorms and Microbursts
summary: No light airplane can fight a thunderstorm or a microburst; the skill is knowing when and how far to stay away.
html:
Ingredients

  1. Sufficient moisture
  2. An unstable lapse rate
  3. An initial lifting force: heating, terrain, a front or converging wind

Life cycle

StageVertical motionKey marker
CumulusUpdrafts throughoutGrowing towering cumulus
MatureUpdrafts and downdrafts side by sideBegins when precipitation starts falling from the cloud base; most intense stage
DissipatingDowndrafts dominateRain tapers, cloud spreads out

A single cell life cycle is often under an hour, but multicell storms and supercells can last for hours.

Hazards

  • Severe turbulence and strong up and down drafts, inside and well outside the cloud
  • Hail, which can fall from the anvil into clear air miles from the core
  • Lightning; vivid and frequent lightning suggests a severe storm
  • Icing in the cloud above the freezing level
  • Gust fronts, wind shear and microbursts near the surface
  • Low ceilings and visibility in heavy rain, plus altimeter errors from rapid pressure changes

Storm organization

  • Squall line: a narrow, nonfrontal band of active storms, often ahead of a cold front. Frequently holds the most severe weather and is too long to go around.
  • Embedded thunderstorms: hidden inside other cloud layers or haze, so you cannot see and avoid them visually.

Microbursts by the numbers

ItemValue
Horizontal sizeDowndraft usually less than 1 mile across; near the ground the outflow can spread to about 2.5 miles in diameter
DowndraftUp to 6,000 feet per minute
Outflow windsUp to about 45 knots each side, so about a 90 knot shear across it
DurationRarely longer than 15 minutes from first contact with the ground

Sequence on approach: headwind (airspeed up, balloon), then downdraft, then tailwind (airspeed and lift collapse). An unexplained airspeed gain near convective weather is your cue to go around immediately.

Avoidance rules worth memorizing

  • Avoid any severe or intense echo thunderstorm by at least 20 nautical miles.
  • Never take off or land in the face of an approaching thunderstorm.
  • Do not fly under a thunderstorm even if you can see through it.
  • Do not fly under the anvil; hail can fall there.
  • Do not trust the visual appearance of a storm to judge its turbulence.
  • Clear the top of a known or suspected severe storm by at least 1,000 feet for each 10 knots of wind speed at the cloud top, which is beyond most light airplanes.
keyFacts: Moisture, unstable lapse rate, lifting force
Precipitation begins falling from the cloud base
About 45 knots each side, 90 knots total
Nonfrontal line of storms, often ahead of a cold front
memoryAids: Thunderstorm recipe: wet, wobbly and a lift.
Microburst: head, down, tail.
Twenty miles from the mean ones.
traps: Saying the mature stage begins with the anvil; it begins when precipitation starts.
Counting only one side of the microburst outflow; the shear is about double.
Treating an airspeed gain near a storm as extra margin rather than a go around cue.
Assuming embedded storms are weak because they are surrounded by cloud.
Racing an approaching storm to take off first.

title: Icing, Frost, Fog and Visibility
summary: Ice ruins the wing and fog ruins the view; both give fair warning if you read temperature, dewpoint and wind.
html:
Structural icing

Two requirements: visible moisture (cloud, rain, drizzle) and an airframe at or below 0 degrees C. Cloud droplets often stay liquid well below freezing (supercooled) and freeze on impact.

TypeHow it formsTypical sourceCharacter
RimeSmall droplets freeze instantly, trapping airStratiform cloudsRough, milky, brittle
ClearLarge drops flow back before freezingCumuliform clouds, freezing rainSmooth, heavy, hard to remove
MixedCombination of the twoVaried drop sizes, often wet snow mixed inRough and hard

Effects: lift down, drag up, weight up, thrust down, and a higher stall speed. Even a thin layer is dangerous.

Freezing level and freezing rain

Find the freezing level from the winds and temperatures aloft by interpolating to 0 degrees C. In Figure 17, STL is plus 2 at 9,000 feet and minus 4 at 12,000 feet, so freezing is near 10,000 feet. Freezing rain means warm air above and subfreezing air below. Descending will not help when the surface is below freezing; leave the area. Ice pellets at the surface mean freezing rain higher up.

Frost

Frost forms by deposition when a surface cools to the dewpoint of the adjacent air and that dewpoint is below freezing. It roughens the wing, disrupts airflow, reduces lift and increases drag. It may prevent the airplane from becoming airborne at normal speed. Remove all frost before flight.

Fog types

FogCauseKey conditions
RadiationGround cools on clear nightsClear sky, light or calm wind, small spread, low lying land; burns off after sunrise
AdvectionMoist air moves over a colder surfaceCoastal areas, wind up to about 15 knots; can persist and spread widely; stronger wind lifts it to stratus
UpslopeMoist, stable air pushed up terrainNeeds wind; lasts as long as the upslope flow
SteamCold air over warmer waterRising wisps; low level turbulence and icing possible
Precipitation inducedWarm rain evaporates into cooler air belowAhead of warm fronts; widespread and long lasting
IceVapor deposits directly as ice crystalsExtreme cold, about minus 25 degrees F or colder

Planning cue: a temperature and dewpoint spread of about 3 degrees C or less and shrinking, with a clear, calm night ahead, means fog is likely.

Other obstructions to visibility

  • Haze: fine particles trapped in stable air. Makes the runway look farther away, so pilots tend to fly a low approach. Visibility is often much worse looking into the sun.
  • Smoke: concentrates under inversions near fires and cities, often thickest in the morning.
  • Volcanic ash: abrasive, can cause engine failure and scour windshields, may be invisible at night and is not reliably detected by airborne radar. Avoid it completely.
  • Blowing dust, sand and snow: strong wind lifts particles; visibility can drop suddenly.
keyFacts: Visible moisture and airframe at or below 0 degrees C
Small droplets, stratiform clouds, rough and milky
Large drops, cumuliform clouds or freezing rain, smooth and heavy
Warm layer aloft over subfreezing air
Surface at or below a dewpoint that is below freezing
Clear, calm night, small spread, low terrain
Moist air over colder surface, wind up to about 15 knots
Moist stable air forced up terrain by wind
Runway looks farther away, leading to a low approach
Avoid; may be invisible and not shown on radar
memoryAids: Rime is rough and from stratus; clear is from cumulus and freezing rain.
Radiation fog is calm and clear; advection fog needs a breeze.
Clean wing or no wing: remove all frost.
traps: Thinking frost will blow off on the takeoff roll.
Descending to escape freezing rain when the surface is below freezing.
Confusing advection fog (wind required) with radiation fog (calm required).
Assuming icing needs a below freezing air temperature only, with no visible moisture.
Believing haze makes the runway look closer; it looks farther away.

title: Getting a Weather Briefing
summary: Know which briefing to ask for, what comes first, and where official weather lives.
html:
Where official weather comes from

The National Weather Service produces the observations, forecasts, and advisories. You get them through Flight Service (phone 1 800 WX BRIEF, or online at 1800wxbrief.com) and through aviationweather.gov, the free site of the NWS Aviation Weather Center. Commercial apps repackage the same data. For a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, 14 CFR 91.103 requires you to become familiar with weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, and alternatives.

The three preflight briefings

BriefingWhen to request it
StandardYou have not had a previous briefing and have not reviewed the weather yourself
AbbreviatedYou need to update an earlier briefing or want only one or two specific items
OutlookDeparture is 6 or more hours away

When you call, say you are a pilot, whether the flight is VFR or IFR, the aircraft number or your name, the aircraft type, departure point, route, destination, altitude, and estimated time of departure and time en route.

Order of a standard briefing

  1. Adverse conditions
  2. VFR flight not recommended, when applicable
  3. Synopsis
  4. Current conditions
  5. En route forecast
  6. Destination forecast
  7. Winds and temperatures aloft
  8. NOTAMs
  9. ATC delays and other information on request

A VFR flight not recommended statement is advisory. You remain the final authority under 91.3, but treat it as a strong warning.

In flight

Flight Service answers on the frequencies printed on sectional charts and in the Chart Supplement; use it for updates, PIREPs, and to open or close a VFR flight plan. The old Flight Watch service on 122.0 was discontinued in 2015.

Closing the loop

A tower never closes a VFR flight plan for you. If you have not closed it within about 30 minutes after your ETA, Flight Service starts looking for you.

Personal minimums

Legal VFR is the floor. Set ceiling, visibility, and wind limits above it and compare every TAF and GFA forecast with them, not just with Part 91.
keyFacts: No prior briefing or self review
Update or a few specific items
First item in a standard briefing
Search starts about 30 minutes after ETA
memoryAids: SAO: Standard, Abbreviated, Outlook, from most to least complete.
Adverse first: the briefer leads with what could make you cancel.
traps: Choosing an outlook briefing for a flight 2 hours away; outlook is for 6 or more hours.

Treating VFR flight not recommended as a legal prohibition.
Answering Flight Watch 122.0 for in flight weather; it no longer exists.

title: Winds Aloft and Pilot Reports
summary: Decode the FB forecast in seconds, handle the over 100 knot code, and pull hazards from a PIREP.
html:
The winds and temperatures aloft forecast (FB)

Levels are MSL; directions are true; speeds are knots; temperatures are degrees C.

CodeDecode
2219-07220 degrees at 19 knots, minus 7 degrees C
2714270 degrees at 14 knots, no temperature given
9900Light and variable, less than 5 knots
239440230 degrees at 94 knots, minus 40 (above 24,000 feet the minus sign is dropped)
730649Direction 73 is impossible: subtract 50 for 230 degrees, add 100 to 06 for 106 knots, minus 49

Why a box is blank

  • No winds are forecast for a level within 1,500 feet of the station elevation (or below it).
  • No temperatures are forecast for the 3,000 foot level, or for any level within 2,500 feet of the station.

So DEN (about 5,400 feet) has nothing at 3,000 or 6,000 feet, and AMA (about 3,600 feet) has a wind but no temperature at 6,000 feet.

Interpolating

For an altitude halfway between two levels, average direction, speed, and temperature. HLC at 7,500 feet: 1707-01 and 2113-03 give about 190 degrees at 10 knots, minus 2 degrees C.

PIREPs

UA is routine and UUA is urgent. Urgent reports cover tornadoes, funnel clouds and waterspouts, severe or extreme turbulence, severe icing, hail, low level wind shear, and volcanic ash. PIREP heights are MSL and times are UTC.

ElementMeaning
/OVLocation; KOKC dash KTUL is a route segment
/TMTime, UTC
/FLAltitude in hundreds of feet MSL
/TPAircraft type
/SKSky cover, base and TOP in hundreds of feet MSL
/TATemperature, degrees C
/WVWind, magnetic direction and speed
/TBTurbulence, intensity and altitudes
/ICIcing, intensity, type, altitudes
/RMRemarks

PIREPs are the only direct observations of tops, icing, and turbulence. Give them whenever you meet something unforecast.

title: AIRMETs, SIGMETs, and CWAs
summary: Match each hazard to the advisory that covers it, and know how long each stays valid.
html:
The advisory ladder

ProductCoversIssued and valid
AIRMET SierraIFR conditions, extensive mountain obscurationEvery 6 hours, valid 6 hours
AIRMET TangoModerate turbulence, sustained surface winds 30 knots or more, nonconvective low level wind shearEvery 6 hours, valid 6 hours
AIRMET ZuluModerate icing, freezing levelsEvery 6 hours, valid 6 hours
SIGMET (nonconvective)Severe icing or severe and extreme turbulence not from thunderstorms, dust or sandstorm below 3 miles, volcanic ashAs needed, valid up to 4 hours (6 for volcanic ash and tropical cyclones)
Convective SIGMETA line of thunderstorms at least 60 miles long with storms along at least 40 percent of it; an area of thunderstorms covering at least 40 percent of the area; embedded or severe thunderstorms expected for more than 30 minutes; tornadoes, surface hail 3/4 inch or larger, or surface wind gusts of 50 knots or moreHourly at 55 minutes past; each bulletin supersedes the last (handbook: valid up to 2 hours; AIM: up to 1 hour)
CWAConditions meeting or approaching any of the above, from the ARTCC Center Weather Service UnitUnscheduled, valid up to 2 hours

Key ideas

  • A convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing, and low level wind shear; those are not issued separately.
  • AIRMETs matter most to light airplanes, but they apply to everyone.
  • G AIRMETs show the same hazards graphically as snapshots at 0, 3, 6, 9, and 12 hours. Read the snapshots on each side of your flight time.
  • A CWA is a short range nowcast that often arrives before a formal SIGMET.

Turning an advisory into a decision

An AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing above a 6,000 foot freezing level does not ground a VFR flight, but it removes the cloud tops and the higher altitudes from your plan. Stay below the freezing level, clear of clouds, with a planned exit, or wait. For thunderstorms, avoid severe cells by at least 20 miles.

Severe icing, severe turbulence, dust, volcanic ash
Up to 4 hours, 6 for volcanic ash or tropical cyclones
Hourly at H+55, each superseding the last

AIRMET is moderate, SIGMET is severe, convective is thunderstorms.

Radar and satellite in one line each

title: Cockpit Weather and Its Limits
summary: Datalink weather is a strategic tool; the picture is always older than it looks.
html:
Sources you can use in the air

  • ATIS: recorded airport information; wind is magnetic.
  • ASOS and AWOS: automated stations, broadcast on a frequency and by phone. AO1 has no precipitation discriminator; AO2 does. Automated CLR means no clouds below 12,000 feet.
  • Flight Service by radio: updates, advisories, and the place to give PIREPs.
  • FIS-B: free broadcast weather through ADS-B In, on the 978 MHz UAT link only.
  • Satellite datalink: commercial, needs a subscription.

FIS-B products and limits

FIS-B provides NEXRAD mosaics, METARs, TAFs, winds aloft, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, convective SIGMETs, PIREPs, and TFRs among others. It relies on line of sight to ground stations, so it often drops out on the ground and at low altitude. A 1090ES Out installation alone does not receive it.

NEXRAD mosaic latency

The time stamp marks when the mosaic was built, not when each radar scanned. Some cells may be much older than the label, and storms can move or grow in the meantime. Never use datalink radar to pick a path between cells. Avoid severe thunderstorms by at least 20 miles and never fly under one.

What radar cannot show

Radar sees precipitation. Clouds without precipitation, fog, icing conditions, and clear air turbulence are invisible to it, so a clean display is not a clear sky.

Habit that saves you

Get a complete briefing before departure, use the cockpit display to watch the big picture, and keep asking Flight Service and ATC. Leave early when the trend turns against you.
keyFacts: Line of sight; lost low or on the ground
Mosaic creation time; data may be older
At least 20 miles from severe cells
memoryAids: Strategic, not tactical: datalink radar plans the route, it does not thread the needle.
ATIS and tower winds are magnetic; METAR, TAF, and winds aloft are true.
traps: Trusting the NEXRAD time stamp as the age of every cell.
Assuming 1090ES Out alone receives FIS-B.
Treating a gap between cells on the display as a safe path.
Thinking radar shows clouds, fog, or icing.

title: Four Forces and Lift
summary: Everything about flying starts with four forces and one angle: the angle of attack.
html:
The four forces

Lift acts perpendicular to the relative wind, weight acts toward the center of the earth, thrust pulls forward, and drag acts rearward, parallel to the relative wind. In straight and level unaccelerated flight they are in balance: lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. Thrust does not have to exceed drag to keep you moving, only to accelerate you.

Airfoil vocabulary

TermMeaning
Chord lineStraight line from leading edge to trailing edge
CamberCurvature of the airfoil above and below the chord line
Relative windAirflow opposite the flight path, regardless of where the nose points
Angle of attackAngle between chord line and relative wind; the pilot controls it with the elevator
Angle of incidenceFixed angle between chord line and longitudinal axis; set at the factory
Center of pressurePoint where the resultant aerodynamic force acts on the wing

How lift is made

Bernoulli: air speeds up over the curved upper surface and its static pressure drops, so pressure is higher under the wing than above it. Newton: the wing turns air downward (downwash) and the air pushes the wing up. These are two views of the same lift, not competing theories.

The lift equation in words

Lift depends on the coefficient of lift (set mostly by angle of attack and flap setting), air density, wing area, and the square of airspeed. Double the airspeed and lift grows four times. To hold altitude while slowing, the pilot must raise the angle of attack; while speeding up, lower it.

The stall

Each wing has a critical angle of attack, a fixed value for a given wing and flap setting. Beyond it the airflow separates from the upper surface and lift drops sharply. That angle does not change with weight, bank, or power. What changes is the airspeed at which you reach it. So a wing can stall at any airspeed, in any attitude, at any power setting.

A gust can stall a wing too: an updraft rotates the relative wind upward, raising the angle of attack without any change in pitch.
keyFacts: Lift equals weight, thrust equals drag
Chord line to longitudinal axis, fixed
Exceeding the critical angle of attack
Same stall angle, higher stall speed
memoryAids: Attack is the angle the pilot can attack with the yoke; incidence is installed in the factory.
Twice the speed, four times the lift.
traps: Thinking thrust must exceed drag in steady cruise.
Confusing angle of attack with pitch attitude or with angle of incidence.
Believing a stall only happens at low airspeed or with the nose high.
Thinking weight changes the critical angle of attack.

title: Drag, Ground Effect, Wake
summary: Know which drag grows with speed, why the airplane floats in ground effect, and where vortices go.
html:
Two kinds of drag

TypeSourceAs airspeed increases
ParasiteForm, skin friction, interferenceIncreases, roughly with speed squared
InducedByproduct of lift, wingtip vortices, rearward tilted liftDecreases

Total drag is lowest where the two curves cross. That speed is L/D max: the best lift to drag ratio, which gives the best power off glide distance. Fly slower than that and induced drag climbs steeply; faster and parasite drag takes over.

Ground effect

Within about one wingspan of the surface, the ground restricts the downwash and the wingtip vortices. Induced drag drops, and the wing needs less angle of attack for the same lift. Parasite drag and the critical angle of attack are unchanged.

  • Landing: excess speed means a long float. Fly the published approach speed.
  • Takeoff: the airplane may lift off below the speed needed to climb. As it rises out of ground effect, induced drag returns and it can settle back or stall. Accelerate in ground effect first, then climb. This is the basis of the soft field takeoff.
  • Airspeed and pitot static readings can also shift slightly in ground effect.

Wingtip vortices

Vortices begin at rotation and end when the nosewheel touches down. They are strongest when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean, and slow. They sink below the flight path, and near the ground they drift outward. A light crosswind can hold the upwind vortex over the runway; a light quartering tailwind can push vortices into your touchdown zone.

SituationAvoidance
Landing behind a large aircraft, same runwayStay at or above its path, land beyond its touchdown point
Departing behind a large aircraftRotate before its rotation point, climb above its path
Crossing behind en routeStay above its flight path
keyFacts: Where induced equals parasite; best glide
Less induced drag, less AOA needed
memoryAids: Induced drag is induced by lift, so it is worst when the wing works hardest: slow.
Land long, lift early: beyond their touchdown, before their rotation.
Heavy, clean, slow makes the vortex grow.
traps: Thinking ground effect increases drag or raises the critical angle of attack.
Climbing out of ground effect before reaching the proper speed.
Landing short of a large aircraft's touchdown point.
Assuming strong winds are the worst case for wake turbulence.

title: Stability and Control
summary: Stability is the airplane's built in wish to fly straight; CG location decides how strong that wish is.
html:
Static versus dynamic

Static stability is the initial tendency after a disturbance: positive returns toward the original attitude, neutral stays in the new attitude, negative diverges further. Dynamic stability is what happens over time: oscillations that dampen are positive, constant oscillations are neutral, growing oscillations are negative.

Three axes

StabilityMotionAbout axisMain source
LongitudinalPitchLateralCG ahead of center of lift, horizontal tail down force
LateralRollLongitudinalDihedral, keel effect, sweepback
DirectionalYawVerticalVertical fin, side area behind the CG

CG and its effects

Most airplanes are slightly nose heavy, and the tail pushes down to balance. That tail down force is extra weight the wing must carry.

ItemForward CGAft CG
Stall speedHigherLower
Cruise speedLowerHigher
StabilityMore stable, heavier pitch forcesLess stable, lighter pitch forces
Stall and spin recoveryEasierHarder, possibly impossible beyond the aft limit

Controls

Adverse yaw: the down aileron on the rising wing adds lift and induced drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn. Coordinated rudder fixes it.

Trim tabs move opposite to the surface. Tab down pushes the elevator trailing edge up, which holds the nose up.

Flaps increase lift and drag, allowing a steeper approach without more airspeed and a lower stall speed. Plain flaps add camber; split flaps hinge from the lower surface; slotted flaps add a gap that energizes the airflow; Fowler flaps slide aft and down, adding area and camber for the largest lift increase. Slots and slats at the leading edge delay separation and let the wing reach a higher angle of attack.
keyFacts: Higher stall speed, more stable, slower cruise
Less stable, harder stall and spin recovery
Nose yaws away from the turn on aileron input
Moves aft and down, adds area and camber
memoryAids: Static is the first step, dynamic is the whole dance.
Forward CG: safe but slow. Aft CG: fast but fragile.
traps: Mixing up static and dynamic stability definitions.
Thinking a forward CG lowers stall speed.
Getting trim tab direction backwards.
Assigning dihedral to directional stability.

title: Turns, Load Factor, Stalls
summary: Bank adds G, G raises stall speed, and the airspeed indicator tells you where the limits are.
html:
What turns the airplane

Banking tilts lift; the horizontal component turns the airplane while the vertical component must still equal weight. So in a level turn total lift, and load factor, must increase. In a coordinated level turn load factor depends only on bank angle: n equals 1 divided by the cosine of the bank.

BankLoad factorStall speed increase
30°1.15 GAbout 7 percent
45°1.41 GAbout 19 percent
60°2.0 GAbout 41 percent
75°About 3.9 GAbout 97 percent

Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor. Example: 50 knot stall speed at 60 degrees is 50 × 1.41, about 71 knots. Load the wings with weight × load factor: 2,000 pounds at 60 degrees means the wings carry 4,000 pounds.

Rate and radius

At a constant airspeed, more bank gives a higher rate and smaller radius. At a constant bank, more airspeed gives a lower rate and larger radius. In a steep turn the outer wing flies faster, creating the overbanking tendency; hold a little opposite aileron.

Steep turns on the checkride

Private ACS: about 45 degrees of bank, altitude within 100 feet, airspeed within 10 knots, bank within 5 degrees, roll out within 10 degrees of entry heading, at or below VA or the manufacturer's speed.

Maneuvering speed and the V G diagram

VA is where the stall line meets the positive limit load on the V G diagram (Figure 72, point C). Below VA, the wing stalls before it can be overstressed by a single full deflection. VA decreases as weight decreases, roughly with the square root of the weight ratio. Normal category limit loads are 3.8 G positive and 1.52 G negative.

Stall types and recovery

  • Accelerated stall: at a higher than normal speed because of load factor, as in a steep turn or abrupt pull.
  • Cross control stall: skidding turn with inside rudder and opposite aileron; the inside wing stalls first and the airplane rolls under. Classic base to final killer.
  • Secondary stall: pulling too hard during recovery.
  • Recovery: reduce angle of attack first, then level the wings, then add power as appropriate.

Airspeed indicator markings (Figure 4)

MarkingMeaningFigure 4
White arc low endVS0, landing configuration stall speedStart of white arc
White arc high endVFE, max flaps extended100 knots
Green arc low endVS1, clean stall speedStart of green arc
Green arc high endVNO, max structural cruise165 knots
Yellow arcCaution range, smooth air only165 to 208 knots
Red lineVNE, never exceed208 knots

VA is not marked on the indicator. Arc values are for maximum weight.

Climb speeds

VX: most altitude per distance, for obstacles. VY: most altitude per time, for normal climbs. With altitude, VX rises and VY falls until they meet at the absolute ceiling.
