VNO to VNE, smooth air only
memoryAids: Sixty degrees, twice the G; stall speed times 1.4.
X marks the spot over the trees: VX for obstacles.
Lighter airplane, lower VA: less mass, less margin.
traps: Thinking higher airspeed changes load factor in a level turn.
Multiplying stall speed by the load factor instead of its square root.
Using the maximum weight VA at light weight.
Reading VNO as the red line or VFE as the top of the green arc.
Swapping VX and VY definitions.

title: Left Turning Tendencies, Spins
summary: Four reasons the nose goes left, and the sequence that gets you out of a spin.
html:
Left turning tendencies

For a propeller turning clockwise as seen from the cockpit, all four push the nose or the wing to the left. They are strongest at high power, low airspeed, and high angle of attack: takeoff and climb.

TendencyMechanismWhen it matters most
TorqueReaction to the propeller's rotation rolls the airplane left (Newton's third law)High power, low speed
Spiraling slipstreamSlipstream wraps around the fuselage and strikes the left side of the vertical finHigh power, low speed
P factorDescending right blade has a higher angle of attack and more thrust than the ascending left bladeHigh angle of attack, climbs
Gyroscopic precessionForce on the propeller disc acts 90° later in the direction of rotationPitch changes, raising the tail in a tailwheel airplane

The fix is right rudder. Fin and engine offsets are set for cruise, so the need grows as speed drops and power increases.

Spins

A spin is an aggravated stall with autorotation. Two ingredients: stall plus yaw. Both wings are stalled, one more deeply, so it drops and the airplane rotates. No stall, no spin. A spiral dive is different: wings not stalled, airspeed rising quickly.

PhaseWhat is happening
EntryStall with yaw, the pilot can still prevent it
IncipientStalled and rotating, not yet stable; about the first two turns in many light airplanes
DevelopedRotation rate, airspeed, and descent rate stabilized
RecoveryAnti spin inputs stop rotation and the wings unstall

PARE recovery (follow the POH when it has a procedure)

  1. Power to idle
  2. Ailerons neutral
  3. Rudder full opposite the rotation
  4. Elevator briskly forward to break the stall

When rotation stops, neutralize the rudder and recover smoothly from the dive without exceeding VNE or the load limits. Use the turn needle or turn coordinator to confirm the direction of rotation; the ball is unreliable in a spin.

Aggravating factors

An aft CG can flatten the spin and make recovery harder or impossible. Power tends to flatten a spin. Spins are prohibited in many normal category airplanes; the checkride covers spin awareness, not spins.
keyFacts: High power, low airspeed, high AOA
Descending right blade makes more thrust
Strikes left side of the vertical fin
Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite, Elevator forward
memoryAids: PARE: Power, Ailerons, Rudder, Elevator.
Climbing with power? Step on the right pedal.
Precession acts 90 degrees ahead, in the direction of rotation.
traps: Saying the ascending blade creates more thrust in P factor.
Saying the slipstream hits the right side of the fin.
Using the ball to determine spin direction.
Confusing a spiral dive (airspeed rising) with a spin (stalled).
Applying aileron against the spin instead of neutral ailerons.

title: Density Altitude
summary: Hot, high, and humid air steals lift, thrust, and power all at once.
html:
Definitions

AltitudeWhat it is
IndicatedRead with the current local altimeter setting
PressureRead with 29.92 set; height above the standard datum plane
DensityPressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature; the altitude the airplane performs at

Standard atmosphere

Sea level: 29.92 inches Hg and 15°C (59°F). Temperature drops about 2°C (3.5°F) per 1,000 feet. Pressure drops about 1 inch Hg per 1,000 feet in the lower atmosphere.

Pressure altitudeStandard temperature
Sea level15°C, 59°F
2,000 ft11°C, 52°F
4,000 ft7°C, 45°F
6,000 ft3°C, 37°F
8,000 ftminus 1°C, 30°F

Computing it

  1. Pressure altitude = field elevation + (29.92 minus altimeter setting) × 1,000. Figure 8's table does this for you: low settings give a positive correction, high settings a negative one.
  2. Density altitude: on Figure 8, enter the bottom at the OAT, go up to the pressure altitude line (interpolate between lines), and read left. Rule of thumb: about 120 feet per degree Celsius above standard.

Example: elevation 5,000 ft, setting 29.62, OAT 30°C. Pressure altitude 5,000 + 300 = 5,300 ft. Standard there is about 4°C, so 26°C warm. 26 × 120 ≈ 3,100, density altitude about 8,400 ft.

What raises density altitude

  • Higher elevation (lower pressure)
  • Higher temperature
  • Higher humidity (water vapor is lighter than dry air)
  • Lower altimeter setting

What high density altitude does

Less power from a normally aspirated engine, less thrust from the propeller, and less lift for a given true airspeed. Takeoff and landing rolls get longer and climb rate drops. Indicated airspeeds for liftoff, approach, and stall stay the same, but the true airspeed and groundspeed at those indicated speeds are higher. Lean the mixture for best power as the POH directs before a high density altitude takeoff.

Risk scenario: a sea level pilot flies into a mountain airport on a summer afternoon with full fuel and passengers. Best options are to depart in the cool early morning, offload weight, and recompute with the charts, not to try the takeoff and see.
keyFacts: Same IAS, higher TAS and groundspeed
memoryAids: Hot, high, humid: all three make the air thin.
Low setting, add altitude; high setting, subtract.
Standard temperature: 15 minus twice the thousands.
traps: Adding the altimeter correction with the wrong sign.
Multiplying the whole OAT by 120 instead of the deviation from standard.
Thinking humid air is denser.
Flying a higher indicated speed to compensate for thin air.

title: Using Performance Charts
summary: Read each chart in the order it was drawn, apply every note, and then add your own margin.
html:
General method

  1. Read the associated conditions box. Power, flaps, runway surface, and technique are assumed.
  2. Compute pressure altitude and get the OAT in the scale the chart wants.
  3. Work left to right through each section, following the guide lines parallel between reference lines.
  4. Apply every note (headwind, tailwind, grass, temperature).
  5. Add a margin. POH numbers come from a new airplane flown by test pilots.

Figure 36: crosswind component

Find the angle between wind and runway (runway 17 is 170°). Follow that angle line out to the wind speed arc. Read down for crosswind and across to the left for headwind. Use the gust value to judge whether you are within the airplane's demonstrated crosswind capability.

Wind angleCrosswind as fraction of wind
30°About one half
45°About seven tenths
60°About nine tenths

Figures 37 and 40: landing and takeoff graphs

Enter at OAT, go up to pressure altitude, across to the first reference line, then follow the guide lines to the weight. Across to the wind reference line, then follow the headwind (or dashed tailwind) lines to the wind component. The value at the next reference line is the ground roll. Follow the obstacle lines to 50 feet for the total over a 50 foot obstacle. Common errors: stopping at the wrong reference line, using the tailwind lines for a headwind, or reading the scale wrong.

Figure 38: landing distance table

  • Pick the column by pressure altitude and temperature.
  • Note 1: decrease 10 percent for each 4 knots of headwind. 8 knots is 20 percent.
  • Note 2: increase 10 percent for each 60°F above standard.
  • Note 3: dry grass adds 20 percent of the total to clear 50 feet to both the ground roll and the total.

Figure 35: power setting table

Choose the block (ISA minus 20°C, standard, ISA plus 20°C) and the pressure altitude row, then read manifold pressure, fuel flow, and true airspeed. Interpolate between rows and blocks when needed. Warmer air needs a little more manifold pressure for the same percent power but yields a higher true airspeed. The shaded rows are full throttle.

Factors at a glance

FactorTakeoff and landing distance
Higher density altitudeLonger
Heavier weightLonger
HeadwindShorter
TailwindMuch longer
Grass, wet, or soft surfaceLonger (landing on wet pavement: less braking)
UpslopeLonger takeoff, shorter landing
Excess approach speedLonger landing
keyFacts: Plus 20 percent of the 50 ft total
Value at the obstacle reference line
Add a margin; test data are best case
memoryAids: Down for cross, across for head.
Every 4 knots of headwind is a 10 percent discount.
traps: Applying the grass correction to the ground roll value instead of the obstacle total.
Taking only one 10 percent step for an 8 knot headwind.
Reading headwind and crosswind backwards on Figure 36.
Stopping at the ground roll when the question asks for distance over a 50 foot obstacle.
Using field elevation instead of pressure altitude.

title: Weight and Balance Fundamentals
summary: Learn the vocabulary and the standard weights that every weight and balance problem is built on.
html:
Why it matters

Every airplane is certificated to fly only within a maximum weight and a CG range. Outside those limits the performance charts no longer apply, stall speeds change, and the airplane may not be controllable. The knowledge test checks that you speak the vocabulary, know the standard weights, and can run the math without slips.

The core terms

TermMeaning
DatumImaginary vertical reference plane chosen by the manufacturer. All arms are measured from it.
Arm (station)Horizontal distance in inches from the datum. Aft is positive, forward is negative.
MomentWeight x arm, in pound inches.
Moment indexMoment divided by a reduction factor such as 100 or 1,000 to keep numbers small.
CGThe balance point: total moment divided by total weight.
CG limitsThe forward and aft boundaries the CG must stay between, often varying with weight.

The weight ladder

WeightWhat it contains
Standard empty weightAirframe, engine, fixed ballast, unusable fuel, full operating fluids including oil
Basic empty weightStandard empty weight plus installed optional equipment
Useful loadMax weight minus basic empty weight: occupants, baggage, usable fuel
PayloadOccupants, baggage, and cargo only (useful load minus usable fuel)
Zero fuel weightLoaded airplane with no usable fuel
Ramp weightTakeoff weight plus fuel for start, taxi, and runup
Max takeoff weightHeaviest weight approved at brake release
Max landing weightHeaviest weight approved for touchdown (often equal to takeoff in light singles)

Some older airplanes list licensed empty weight, which excludes most of the oil. That is why you must read the notes on each chart: some empty weights include oil and some do not.

Standard weights

ItemWeight
Avgas6 lb per gallon
Jet A6.7 lb per gallon
Engine oil7.5 lb per gallon (1.875 lb per quart)
Water8.35 lb per gallon

Quick conversions

  • 4 quarts = 1 gallon. Six quarts of oil = 1.5 gal x 7.5 = 11.25 lb.
  • Gallons to pounds: multiply by 6. Pounds to gallons: divide by 6.
  • Moment index back to moment: multiply by the reduction factor.

Worked mini example

Max takeoff weight 2,550 lb, basic empty weight 1,642 lb. Useful load = 908 lb. With 53 gal (318 lb) of usable fuel, payload = 590 lb. Ramp weight with 1.5 gal for taxi = takeoff weight + 9 lb.

Usable fuel is useful load. Unusable fuel is empty weight. Never mix them.
keyFacts: Max weight minus basic empty weight
Unusable fuel, full oil, optional equipment
Takeoff weight plus taxi and runup fuel
Manufacturer chosen reference plane for all arms
Aft of datum positive, forward negative
memoryAids: Six for gas, seven and a half for oil.
Ramp, then takeoff, then landing: each one lighter by the fuel burned.
traps: Entering fuel in gallons as if they were pounds.
Using 7.5 lb per gallon for fuel or 6 lb per gallon for oil.
Adding oil when the chart says it is already in the empty weight.
Confusing useful load with payload.
Treating a moment index as an arm in inches.

title: Computing CG with Tables and Graphs
summary: Run a full loading problem on the test supplement's tables and graphs, step by step, without the classic slips.
html:
The method in five steps

  1. List every item: empty weight, front seats, rear seats, baggage, fuel (and oil only if the chart says it is not in empty weight).
  2. Look up or compute the moment for each item (weight x arm, or the table or graph value).
  3. Add all weights. Check against maximum weight first.
  4. Add all moments. Divide total moment by total weight for the CG, or compare the moment to the limits directly.
  5. Check the result against the envelope for takeoff, then again for landing after the fuel burn.

Worked example, Figures 32 and 33

Front seats 150 and 160 lb, rear seat 190 lb, baggage 40 lb, main tanks 35 gal.

ItemWeightMoment/100
Empty weight (oil included)2,0151,554
Front 150 lb150128
Front 160 lb160136
Rear 190 lb190230
Baggage 40 lb4056
Main fuel 35 gal210158
Total2,7652,262

Figure 33 at 2,765 lb gives about 2,216 minimum and 2,354 maximum. 2,262 is between them, so the CG is within limits. The actual CG is 226,200 / 2,765 = 81.8 in.

Reading Figure 32 and 33 correctly

  • The occupant tables come in 10 lb steps. For an odd weight, interpolate or compute weight x arm / 100.
  • The CG limit table narrows as weight rises: 77.0 to 85.7 at 2,475 lb or less, 82.1 to 84.7 at 2,950 lb.
  • Figure 33 does the comparison for you: above the maximum moment means aft of limits, below the minimum means forward.

Figure 34: the graph method

Enter the loading graph at each load weight on the left, go across to that item's line, then drop down to read moment/1,000. Add everything, including the empty weight moment, and plot total weight against total moment on the envelope below.

Load lineMoment/1,000 per 100 lb, approximately
Pilot and front passenger3.7
Fuel (6 lb per gal)4.8
Rear passengers7.3
Baggage or child seat (120 lb max)9.3
  • Fuel dots: 38 gal standard (228 lb, about 11.0), 48 gal long range (288 lb, about 13.8).
  • Oil is NOT in this empty weight: add 15 lb at minus 0.2.
  • Max weight 2,300 lb normal category. The dashed utility envelope stops at 2,000 lb.

Figure 67: the chart method

  • Empty weight 2,110 lb, moment/100 1,652, oil included.
  • Rear seats have two columns: forward position arm 111, aft position arm 136. Use the column the question names.
  • Fuel at arm 75, baggage at arm 150. Envelope tops out near 3,400 lb.
  • Compute CG = moment x 100 / weight, then find the point using the weight scale on the right and the CG scale at the bottom.

Always check landing too

Fuel burned comes off at the fuel arm. In these airplanes the fuel is forward of the loaded CG, so the CG moves aft as fuel burns. A loading near the aft limit at takeoff can be outside it at landing.

Front 85, rear 121, baggage 140, main fuel 75, aux fuel 94
Not in empty weight: add 15 lb at minus 0.2

Above max moment means aft; below min moment means forward.
traps: Reading the wrong line on the Figure 34 loading graph.

Forgetting the oil on Figure 34, or adding it on Figures 32 and 67.

title: Shifting, Adding, and Removing Weight
summary: Two short formulas fix almost any out of limits loading; know which one to use and which way the CG moves.
html:
Shifting weight

When weight moves inside the airplane, total weight stays the same and only the moment changes.

Weight shifted / total weight = CG change / distance shifted
  • CG change = weight shifted x distance / total weight.
  • Weight to move = total weight x CG change / distance.
  • The distance is the difference between the two stations, not either station alone.
  • The CG moves in the same direction the weight moves.

Example: 3,200 lb airplane, CG 1.0 in. too far aft. Move baggage from station 150 to station 85, a 65 in. move. Weight to move = 3,200 x 1.0 / 65 = 49 lb.

Adding or removing weight

The cleanest method is to recompute: new moment divided by new weight.

  1. Old moment = old weight x old CG.
  2. Add (or subtract) the item's weight x arm.
  3. Add (or subtract) the item's weight from total weight.
  4. New CG = new moment / new weight.

Example: 2,000 lb at 80 in., add 100 lb at 150 in. New moment 175,000, new weight 2,100, new CG 83.3 in.

Example: 2,900 lb at 88 in., remove 90 lb at 150 in. New moment 241,700, new weight 2,810, new CG 86.0 in.

ActionCG moves
Add weight aft of the CGAft
Add weight forward of the CGForward
Remove weight aft of the CGForward
Remove weight forward of the CG (for example, burn fuel at arm 75)Aft

Beam problems, Figures 60 and 61

Treat the fulcrum as the datum. Everything on one side makes moments that try to tip it one way, everything on the other side the other way. Balance means the two totals are equal.

  • Figure 60: do not forget the 200 lb plank. Its CG is 15 in. right of the fulcrum, so it adds 3,000 in lb to the right side.
  • Figure 61: X is 50 in. left, Y is 25 in. left, Z is 100 in. right of the fulcrum. Use negative arms on the left if you need a system CG.
  • To fix an imbalance by moving one weight, divide the excess moment by that weight. To fix it by removing weight at one spot, divide the excess moment by that spot's arm.

Fixing an out of limits airplane

  • Over weight: remove fuel, baggage, or a passenger. Fuel to drain = excess pounds / 6, rounded up.
  • Aft CG: move weight forward (rear passenger to a front seat, baggage to the cabin). Draining fuel in these airplanes makes it worse.
  • Forward CG: move weight aft or add ballast aft. Transferring fuel to an aft tank (Figure 32 auxiliary tanks at arm 94) helps without changing weight.
keyFacts: Weight shifted / total weight = CG change / distance
CG moves the way the weight moves
New CG = new total moment / new total weight
X 50 left, Y 25 left, Z 100 right of fulcrum
memoryAids: Small over big equals small over big: weight moved over total weight equals CG moved over distance moved.
The CG chases the weight.
traps: Using a station number instead of the distance between stations.
Dividing by the old total weight after adding or removing weight.
Ignoring the plank weight in Figure 60.
Draining fuel to cure an aft CG when the fuel is forward of the CG.
Rounding fuel to drain down instead of up.

title: How Weight and CG Change the Airplane
summary: Forward and aft CG trade stability against performance; overweight steals margin everywhere.
html:
Why CG matters aerodynamically

In a conventional airplane the CG sits ahead of the wing's center of lift, so the nose wants to drop. The horizontal tail pushes down to balance it. That tail down force acts like extra weight the wing has to carry. The farther forward the CG, the more down force is needed.

Forward versus aft CG

EffectForward CGAft CG
Longitudinal stabilityMore stableLess stable
Stall speedHigherLower
Cruise speedLower (more induced drag)Higher
Elevator forcesHeavierLighter, easy to overcontrol
Main riskNot enough elevator to rotate or flareDifficult or impossible stall and spin recovery
  • The forward limit is set by elevator authority at low speed: rotation and the landing flare.
  • The aft limit is set by stability and the ability to recover from stalls and spins.
  • The critical angle of attack does not change with CG. The stall speed does, because the wing must make more lift.

Overweight effects

  • Higher takeoff speed and longer takeoff roll
  • Reduced rate and angle of climb, lower service ceiling
  • Higher stall speed and higher approach and landing speeds
  • Longer landing roll and more brake and tire wear
  • Reduced range and endurance; structural loads closer to limits, especially in turbulence and maneuvering

An overweight airplane does not get legal just because it flies. The performance charts were built at or below max weight, so all of your planned numbers are wrong.

Risk management

  • Use real weights. People and bags are usually heavier than reported.
  • Leave margin below the limits, especially on a hot day or a short runway.
  • Check the landing CG. As forward fuel burns, the CG moves aft.
  • Secure baggage. A shifting load in turbulence moves the CG in flight.
keyFacts: Elevator authority to rotate and flare
Stability and stall or spin recovery
Higher speed, longer run, poorer climb
memoryAids: Forward is safer but slower; aft is faster but riskier.
Nose heavy: heavy tail load, heavy wing, higher stall.
traps: Thinking forward CG lowers stall speed.
Attributing the flare problem to an aft CG.
Believing a within weight loading is automatically within CG limits.
Believing the critical angle of attack changes with CG.

title: The Piston Engine
summary: How the engine makes power, what mixture does to it, and the two kinds of abnormal combustion the test loves.
html:
The four stroke cycle

  1. Intake: piston moves down, intake valve open, fuel air charge drawn in.
  2. Compression: both valves closed, piston moves up and squeezes the charge.
  3. Power: spark plugs fire just before top center; burning gases drive the piston down.
  4. Exhaust: exhaust valve opens, piston moves up and pushes out the burned gas.

Each cylinder has two spark plugs, fed by two independent magnetos. Dual ignition gives redundancy and a more complete, even burn.

Mixture and altitude

A carburetor meters fuel to the volume of air flowing through it. As you climb, each volume of air weighs less, so the same fuel makes the mixture richer. Too rich means lost power, rough running, and fouled plugs. Lean in the climb and cruise as the POH directs.

Going the other way, descending with a mixture leaned for altitude makes it leaner as the air gets denser. Enrich before you need full power, for example before landing and any possible go around.

High density altitude takeoffs: many POHs call for leaning at full throttle for best power before takeoff. Follow the book for your airplane.

Detonation versus preignition

DetonationPreignition
WhatCharge explodes instead of burning smoothly, after the normal sparkCharge ignites before the spark
Triggered byExcess heat and pressure in the cylinderA hot spot: glowing carbon, cracked plug insulator
Common causesFuel grade too low, mixture too lean, high power at low airspeed, long climbs, overheatingHot spots in the chamber, often together with detonation
FixLower the nose for airspeed and cooling, enrich, reduce power, open cowl flapsSame cooling actions, then maintenance

Oil and cooling

Oil lubricates, cools, seals, and cleans. Check the oil pressure gauge right after start: if it does not rise within the POH time limit, shut down. In flight, low pressure with rising temperature means trouble; plan to land.

Air cooled engines depend on airflow. High oil or cylinder head temperature comes from:

  • Low oil quantity
  • Long climbs at low airspeed or high power
  • A mixture too lean
  • Cowl flaps closed, or a blocked oil cooler

Cowl flaps: open for ground ops, takeoff, and climb; close as needed in cruise and descent to avoid overcooling.

Starting and propeller safety

  • Position the airplane so the propeller blast does not hit people, hangars, or other aircraft.
  • Shout "clear" and wait for an answer; look all around before engaging the starter.
  • Treat every propeller as live. A broken P lead leaves a magneto hot even with the key off.
  • Hand propping: a qualified person at the controls, brakes set or wheels chocked, standard callouts repeated back, ignition off while positioning the blades.
keyFacts: Just before top center on compression
Ignition before the spark from a hot spot
More airspeed, richer mixture, less power, cowl flaps open
Shut down within POH time limit
memoryAids: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow: intake, compression, power, exhaust.
Pre means before: preignition happens before the spark.
Climbing up makes it rich; coming down makes it lean.
traps: Confusing detonation (after the spark) with preignition (before the spark).
Leaning further to fight high temperatures; extra fuel is what cools the cylinders.
Thinking a mixture becomes leaner as you climb; it becomes richer.
Closing cowl flaps during a hot climb.
Assuming a propeller is safe because the key is off.

title: Carburetor, Fuel, and Induction Icing
summary: Why carburetors ice, how to recognize it, and how to keep the right fuel, and only fuel, in the tanks.
html:
Carburetor versus fuel injection

A float type carburetor mixes fuel and air in a venturi. The pressure drop and fuel vaporization there can cool the air by as much as 60 degrees F, freezing moisture onto the throttle valve and venturi.

Fuel injection sprays fuel at each intake port. No venturi icing, better fuel distribution, and less tendency to ice. Drawbacks: harder hot starts and possible vapor lock on hot days. Injected engines still have an alternate air source in case impact ice blocks the air filter.

Carburetor ice: when

  • Most likely below about 70 degrees F with relative humidity above about 80 percent
  • Possible in outside temperatures up to about 100 degrees F with high humidity
  • Low power settings are most prone, because the throttle is nearly closed and little engine heat is available

Carburetor ice: how it shows

PropellerFirst signThen
Fixed pitchLoss of RPMEngine roughness
Constant speedDrop in manifold pressure (RPM held by governor)Engine roughness

Carburetor heat

Carb heat routes air heated by the exhaust around the filter into the carburetor. The heated air is less dense, which enrichens the mixture and reduces power. Because the air is unfiltered, avoid it on the ground on dusty surfaces.

  • Ice present: RPM drops at first (possible roughness as water passes through), then gradually rises as the ice melts.
  • No ice: RPM drops and stays down until heat is removed.
  • Use full heat, not partial, unless a carburetor air temperature gauge is installed and the POH says otherwise.
  • Apply before reducing power for a long descent, as most POHs direct.

Fuel grades

GradeColor
80Red
100LLBlue
100Green
Jet AClear or straw

If the approved grade is not available, use only a higher grade the manufacturer allows. A lower grade invites detonation.

Contamination and sumping

  • Water is heavier than fuel and sinks to the drains. Sample every drain before the first flight and after fueling.
  • Keep draining until the samples are clean. Check color and smell; clear fuel smelling of kerosene in a piston airplane means jet fuel. Do not fly.
  • Filling tanks after the last flight of the day reduces condensation.

Vapor lock and fuel starvation

Vapor lock is fuel boiling in the lines, usually on a hot day or with a hot engine, blocking the flow. An electric boost pump helps where installed. Power loss soon after a tank switch points to the selector; go back to the tank that was working.
keyFacts: Below 70 degrees F, humidity above 80 percent
Up to about 100 degrees F if humid
Use a higher approved grade only
memoryAids: Ice drops, then rises; no ice, it drops and stays down.
Blue is what you will usually see: 100LL.
traps: Assuming ice cannot form when it is warm outside.
Expecting an RPM drop as the first sign in a constant speed propeller airplane.
Thinking fuel injection is immune to all induction icing; impact ice can still block the filter.
Using a lower fuel grade in a pinch.
Stopping after one clean looking sample when contamination was found.

title: Ignition, Electrical, and Propellers
summary: Magnetos that run without the battery, an electrical system that runs out of battery, and a propeller with two levers.
html:
Magnetos

Magnetos are engine driven generators that make their own spark. They need no battery or alternator; the master switch does not affect them. The ignition switch stops a magneto by grounding it through its P lead.

The mag check

  • At runup RPM, select L, back to BOTH, then R, back to BOTH.
  • Expect a small, smooth drop on each, within the POH limits for drop and difference.
  • No drop at all: suspect an ungrounded magneto. It may be hot with the key off. Get it checked.
  • Large drop or roughness: possible fouled plug or bad magneto. A runup to burn off fouling may be allowed by the POH; otherwise, maintenance.

Electrical system

Most light airplanes have a 14 or 28 volt DC system. An engine driven alternator supplies power and charges the battery; it produces good output even at low RPM. Older generators often cannot keep up at idle.

  • Master switch: connects the battery and alternator field to the bus.
  • Bus bar: distribution point that feeds individual circuits.
  • Circuit breakers or fuses: protect wiring from overcurrent. Reset a popped breaker once after a short wait; if it pops again, leave it.

Ammeter versus loadmeter

GaugeShowsNormal
Center zero ammeterCurrent into (+) or out of (minus) the batterySlight plus after start, near zero in cruise
LoadmeterLoad on the alternator onlySome positive load; cannot show discharge

Alternator failure

  1. Recognize: low voltage light, ammeter discharge, or loadmeter at zero.
  2. Follow the checklist: check breakers, try the reset the POH allows.
  3. Shed nonessential load: extra radios, lights you do not need, pitot heat if not needed.
  4. Land at the nearest suitable airport; the battery will run down.

The engine keeps running on magnetos, but electric instruments, radios, flaps, and lights will go when the battery is flat.

Propellers

A propeller is a rotating wing. It is twisted: blade angle is larger at the hub and smaller at the tip because the tip moves much faster, which keeps angle of attack more even.

Fixed pitchConstant speed
Power indicatorTachometer (RPM)Manifold pressure gauge
ControlsThrottleThrottle sets manifold pressure; propeller control sets RPM
EfficiencyBest at one speedGood across climb and cruise
  • Avoid high manifold pressure with low RPM: excessive cylinder pressure.
  • Increase power: mixture, propeller, throttle. Decrease power: throttle, propeller, mixture.
  • Low blade angle (high RPM) for takeoff; higher blade angle for cruise.
keyFacts: High manifold pressure with low RPM
memoryAids: Power up: prop before throttle. Power down: throttle before prop.
Magnetos make their own spark: the key, not the master, kills them.
traps: Thinking the master switch shuts down the ignition.
Reading a loadmeter as if it could show a discharge.
Treating a perfect mag check with zero drop as good news.
Resetting a circuit breaker repeatedly.
Moving the throttle up before the propeller when adding power.

title: Airframe Systems: Gear, Brakes, Environment, Oxygen, Ice
summary: The supporting systems: trim, brakes and hydraulics, cabin heat, oxygen, and what ice protection really means.
html:
Trim tabs

A trim tab moves opposite to the surface it trims. Nose up trim: tab down, elevator trailing edge held up. An antiservo tab on a stabilator moves in the same direction to add feel.

Landing gear and brakes

  • Configurations: tricycle (nosewheel) and conventional (tailwheel); fixed or retractable.
  • Most light airplanes steer with a nosewheel linked to the rudder pedals, plus differential braking.
  • Brakes are hydraulic: each toe pedal works its own master cylinder for its own main wheel.
  • Spongy pedal, low pedal, or a fluid puddle near the wheel: get maintenance before flight.

Hydraulic basics

A hydraulic system uses an incompressible fluid to transmit force: a pump or master cylinder, lines, and an actuator. In light airplanes you meet it in brakes and in some retractable gear and flap systems.

Environmental: heat and carbon monoxide

Cabin heat usually comes from air passed through a shroud around the exhaust muffler. A crack lets carbon monoxide into the cabin. Symptoms: headache, drowsiness, dizziness, and eventually loss of muscle power. Response: heat off, fresh air open, oxygen if available, land. A CO detector is cheap insurance.

Oxygen

Cabin pressure altitude (91.211)Requirement
Above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 feet MSLRequired crew uses oxygen for time beyond 30 minutes
Above 14,000 feet MSLRequired crew uses oxygen the entire time
Above 15,000 feet MSLEach occupant must be provided oxygen
  • System types: continuous flow (cannula or mask), diluter demand, pressure demand, and electronic pulse demand.
  • Use aviator's breathing oxygen: very dry, so it will not freeze in valves. Not medical or welding oxygen.
  • Keep oil, grease, and open flame away from oxygen; it makes things burn fiercely.

Ice protection

TypePurposeExamples
Anti icingPrevents ice from formingPitot heat, heated windshield, propeller anti ice, fluid systems
DeicingRemoves ice after it formsPneumatic boots, some electric propeller boots

Pitot heat alone does not approve an airplane for flight into known icing. The POH and placards say whether it is approved.
keyFacts: Each toe pedal has its own master cylinder
Very low moisture, will not freeze
memoryAids: Oxygen: 12.5 for 30 minutes, 14 always for crew, 15 for everyone.
Anti means against forming; de means removing what formed.
traps: Calling pneumatic boots anti icing.
Treating pitot heat as an approval for known icing.
Applying the above 15,000 occupant rule to the crew at 13,500.
Leaving cabin heat on when CO symptoms appear.

title: Pitot Static Instruments and Errors
summary: Read the airspeed and altimeter faces cold, know every blockage cold, and never get caught by high to low.
html:
Which instrument uses what

InstrumentPitotStatic
Airspeed indicatorYesYes
AltimeterNoYes
Vertical speed indicatorNoYes

Airspeed indicator markings

MarkingMeaning
Bottom of white arcVS0, stall in landing configuration
Top of white arcVFE, maximum flap extended speed
Bottom of green arcVS1, stall in a specified configuration (usually clean)
Top of green arcVNO, maximum structural cruising speed
Yellow arcCaution range, smooth air only
Red lineVNE, never exceed

In Figure 4 the white arc ends at 100 knots and the green arc ends at about 165 knots. Maneuvering speed and VY are not marked.

Reading a three pointer altimeter

  • Long, thin pointer: hundreds of feet.
  • Wide pointer: thousands of feet.
  • Slim pointer: ten thousands. In Figure 3 it is short; in Figure 82 it is a thin pointer that reaches the rim with a small triangle tip.
  • Read the ten thousands pointer first, but check it against the thousands pointer. If the thousands pointer is halfway between 9 and 0, you are at 9,500, not 10,500, even though the ten thousands pointer is almost on 1.
  • On altimeters with a crosshatch flag (Figure 82), the stripes show whenever you are below 10,000 feet.

Blockages

BlockageAirspeedAltimeterVSI
Pitot ram blocked, drain openDrops to zeroNormalNormal
Pitot ram and drain blockedActs like an altimeter: rises in a climb, falls in a descentNormalNormal
Static ports blockedReads low in a climb, high in a descentFrozenZero

Alternate static source (cabin air in an unpressurized airplane) is at slightly lower pressure: the altimeter and airspeed read a little high, and the VSI shows a momentary climb when you switch.

Altimeter errors

  • Pressure: flying from high pressure to low pressure without resetting, the altimeter reads higher than true altitude. Each inch of setting is about 1,000 feet.
  • Temperature: in air colder than standard, true altitude is lower than indicated. Warmer than standard, true altitude is higher.
  • Setting the window: if the setting is too low, the altimeter reads too low; too high, it reads too high.

Types of altitude

AltitudeDefinition
IndicatedRead directly with the current local setting
PressureIndicated with 29.92 set; height above the standard datum plane
DensityPressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature; drives performance
TrueActual height above mean sea level
AbsoluteActual height above the ground (AGL)
keyFacts: Altimeter frozen, VSI zero, airspeed low in climb
Altimeter and airspeed read slightly high
memoryAids: High to low, or hot to cold, look out below.
Altimeter setting goes the way the needle goes: set it higher, it reads higher.
White is for wheels and flaps down; green is for going; yellow is for caution; red is dead.
traps: Reading 10,500 when the thousands pointer shows you are still at 9,500.
Swapping the top of the white arc (VFE) with the top of the green arc (VNO).
Mixing up pitot blocked with the drain open (zero) and drain closed (acts like an altimeter).
Forgetting that temperature errors work like pressure errors: cold air means lower than indicated.
Thinking the alternate static source reads lower.

title: Gyroscopic Instruments, Vacuum, and Glass
summary: Which gyro runs on what, how each one fails, and how glass cockpits replace them.
html:
Two gyro principles

  • Rigidity in space: a spinning gyro holds its orientation. Used by the attitude indicator and the heading indicator.
  • Precession: a force applied to a spinning gyro shows up 90 degrees ahead in the direction of rotation. Used by the turn coordinator; also the cause of heading indicator drift.

The three gyro instruments

InstrumentTypical powerShows
Attitude indicatorVacuumPitch and bank
Heading indicatorVacuumHeading; must be set to the compass
Turn coordinatorElectricRate of roll and turn, plus the ball for coordination; no pitch

Attitude indicator (Figure 7)

A is the bank index, B the horizon bar (gyro driven), C the miniature airplane (fixed to the case). Read attitude by comparing C to B. When the horizon is high on the right, the airplane is banked right. Typical bank scale marks are 10, 20, 30, 60, and 90 degrees, and many instruments also mark 45.

Heading indicator (Figure 6)

Read the heading under the top index (the nose of the airplane symbol). It drifts from precession and the earth's rotation, so reset it to the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes, in straight, level, unaccelerated flight.

Turn coordinator versus turn and slip

The turn coordinator's gyro is canted, so it senses roll as well as yaw; the turn and slip indicator shows rate of turn only. Wingtip on the index: standard rate, 3 degrees per second, 360 degrees in 2 minutes. The ball shows slip or skid: step on the ball.

Vacuum failure

  • Clues: suction gauge low, attitude and heading indicators slowly drifting, sometimes a warning flag.
  • Electric turn coordinator, airspeed, altimeter, and VSI still agree on what the airplane is really doing.
  • Cover the failed instruments and fly partial panel. In clouds this is an emergency; tell ATC.

Glass cockpit

UnitProvides
AHRS (attitude and heading reference system)Attitude, heading, and rate of turn from solid state sensors and a magnetometer
ADC (air data computer)Airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, and temperature from pitot, static, and OAT probes
PFD and MFDDisplay the data; reversionary mode puts the PFD on the remaining screen
  • A red X over a display means that data is invalid. Identify the failed source: attitude red X means AHRS; airspeed and altitude tapes red X means ADC.
  • A pitot or static blockage still fools the ADC exactly as it fools round gauges.
  • Know your standby instruments and their power source, and keep hand flying skills sharp.
keyFacts: Reset to compass about every 15 minutes
Low suction, drifting attitude and heading
PFD shown on the remaining display
memoryAids: Turn time at standard rate: degrees divided by 3 equals seconds.
Step on the ball to center it.
AHRS for attitude, ADC for air.
traps: Thinking the turn coordinator shows pitch.
Reading a heading from the bottom of the heading indicator card.
Trusting a drifting attitude indicator after vacuum loss instead of the agreeing instruments.
Blaming the ADC for an attitude red X.
Resetting the heading indicator during a turn or acceleration.

title: The Magnetic Compass
summary: The one instrument that needs nothing but works only when you understand its lies.
html:
How it works

Two magnets on a float, in a bowl of fluid, align with the earth's magnetic field. It needs no power and no vacuum, so it is the last heading reference standing.

Variation and deviation

ErrorCauseWhere to find it
VariationTrue north and magnetic north are in different placesIsogonic lines on the sectional
DeviationThe airplane's own metal and electrical fieldsCompass correction card

Converting: true heading, apply variation (east is least, west is best: subtract east, add west) to get magnetic heading, then apply the card to get compass heading.

Reading the card (Figure 58)

"For" is the magnetic heading you want; "Steer" is what the compass must read. For 060, steer 056. Working backward: steering 274 puts you on magnetic 270.

Example: true course 128, wind correction 7 degrees right gives true heading 135; variation 15 degrees east gives magnetic 120; the card says steer 116.

Magnetic dip errors

The earth's field dips toward the ground nearer the poles, pulling down on the compass magnets. That causes two errors in the Northern Hemisphere:

Acceleration error (east and west headings)

ANDS: Accelerate, North; Decelerate, South. The error is greatest on east and west headings and does not appear on north or south.

Turning error (north and south headings)

Turn starting fromCompass showsRolling out on it
NorthInitially turns the opposite way, then lagsUndershoot: roll out early
SouthTurns the correct way but faster, leadsOvershoot: roll out late
East or westAbout correctNo lead or lag needed

Other limits

  • Oscillation in turbulence; read an average.
  • Read it only in straight, level, unaccelerated flight.
  • Electrical equipment on or off can change deviation; the card says what was on when it was swung.
keyFacts: True versus magnetic north; isogonic lines
Compass first shows the opposite direction
memoryAids: East is least, west is best.
ANDS: accelerate north, decelerate south.
UNOS: undershoot north, overshoot south.
For is what you want; Steer is what you read.
traps: Confusing variation (geography) with deviation (the airplane).
Applying the correction card backward.
Expecting acceleration error on north or south headings.
Leading the rollout when turning onto south.
Forgetting the wind correction angle before applying variation.

title: Charts, Latitude and Longitude, and Time
summary: Measure a true course and a distance on a sectional the way the test expects, find a point by its coordinates, and convert local time to UTC without slipping an hour.
html:
Measuring a course on a sectional

The test figures are sectional excerpts. Every course you measure on them is a true course, because the grid lines are true meridians and parallels.

  1. Draw or imagine a straight line from the center of the departure airport symbol to the center of the destination symbol.
  2. Put the plotter's center hole on a meridian (a north south line of longitude) near the middle of the route. Do not use the page edge.
  3. Read the scale that matches the general direction. A route toward the northeast must read between 000 and 090. If you get 218 for a northeast route, you read the reciprocal.
  4. For routes close to north or south, the line runs almost along the meridian, so measure against a parallel using the inner scale instead.

Some figures, such as 24, 25 and 71, are printed sideways. Find north from a meridian label like 96° or 121° before measuring, or the answer will be about 90° off.

Distance

Each excerpt has its own nautical mile, statute mile and kilometer scale because the page is not printed at true sectional scale. Use the nautical mile bar for knots problems. Also, one minute of latitude is one nautical mile anywhere on earth, so the tick marks along a meridian are a built in ruler for north south distances.

ConversionFactor
Nautical miles to statute milesmultiply by 1.15
Statute miles to nautical milesmultiply by 0.87
Knots to mphmultiply by 1.15
1 degree of latitude60 NM
1 minute of latitude1 NM

Latitude and longitude

Latitude is measured north of the equator along a meridian; longitude is measured west of Greenwich along a parallel. Over the United States longitude numbers grow toward the west, so 98°06'W is just east of 98°10'W. The minute ticks between labeled lines are at 1 minute intervals, with a longer tick every 10 minutes.

VFR cruising altitude

Magnetic courseAbove 3,000 ft AGL
0° through 179°Odd thousands plus 500 (3,500, 5,500, 7,500)
180° through 359°Even thousands plus 500 (4,500, 6,500, 8,500)

The rule uses magnetic course, not heading and not true course. Convert the measured true course with the isogonic line first.

Time and UTC

Flight plans, weather and ATC use UTC (Zulu). Figure 27 gives the hours to add:

ZoneStandardDaylight
Easternadd 5add 4
Centraladd 6add 5
Mountainadd 7add 6
Pacificadd 8add 7

For an arrival time in another zone, convert the departure time to UTC, add the time en route, then convert to the destination's local time.

Checkpoints for pilotage

Choose features that are big and unique: a highway and railroad crossing beside a town, a dam, a distinctive lake shape. Avoid single small ponds in lake country or lone towers.
keyFacts: Measured against a meridian on the sectional
memoryAids: East is odd, West is even (plus 500 feet) for VFR cruising altitudes.
Sanity check every course: a northeast trip must read between 000 and 090.
traps: Reading the reciprocal scale on the plotter and getting a course 180° off.
Measuring a sideways figure against the page edge instead of a meridian.
Using the statute mile bar for a knots problem.
Choosing cruising altitude from true course or heading instead of magnetic course.
Adding the standard time offset during daylight time, which is off by one hour.

title: Dead Reckoning and the Wind Triangle
summary: Turn a plotted line into a compass heading, a time and a fuel number, then use the 1 in 60 rule to fix errors in flight.
html:
From true course to compass heading

StepApplyResult
True course (TC)plus right WCA, minus left WCATrue heading (TH)
True headingplus west variation, minus east variationMagnetic heading (MH)
Magnetic headingapply compass card deviationCompass heading (CH)

Variation is the angle between true and magnetic north and comes from the dashed magenta isogonic line on the chart. Deviation is the error caused by the airplane's own magnetic fields and comes from the compass card. Read the card as written: FOR 120 STEER 123 means add 3° near 120°.

The wind triangle

Figure 68 shows the classic plot. Start at a point, draw the wind vector downwind (C to A), then swing the true airspeed vector from its end to the course line (A to B). The line along the desired track (C to B) gives true course and groundspeed. The angle between heading and course is the wind correction angle.

  • The airplane always points into the wind: wind from the right means a right correction and a heading greater than the course.
  • A headwind component lowers groundspeed; a tailwind raises it. A direct crosswind still lowers groundspeed slightly because part of the airspeed is used to hold the crab.
  • Quick estimate: maximum crab in degrees is about crosswind divided by true airspeed, times 60. At 100 knots, a 20 knot direct crosswind needs about 12°.

Time, speed, distance, fuel

Time equals distance divided by groundspeed. At 120 knots you cover 2 NM a minute; at 90 knots 1.5 NM a minute; at 60 knots 1 NM a minute. Fuel equals time in hours times gallons per hour.

VFR fuel reserve (91.151)Minimum beyond first intended landing point
Day30 minutes at normal cruise
Night45 minutes at normal cruise

These are legal minimums. Real planning adds taxi, climb and a personal reserve, and fuel is rechecked at each checkpoint against actual groundspeed.

The 1 in 60 rule

One mile off course after 60 miles is a 1° error. So track error in degrees equals miles off times 60 divided by miles flown. To get back to the destination rather than just fly parallel, add a closing angle: miles off times 60 divided by miles remaining.

Example: 3 NM left after 30 NM with 60 NM to go. Track error 6°, closing angle 3°, turn 9° right.

Planned versus actual

Time two checkpoints a known distance apart to get groundspeed. 12 NM in 8 minutes is 90 knots. A groundspeed well below plan means the wind is not as forecast, so revise ETA and fuel at once.
keyFacts: TC, WCA, TH, variation, MH, deviation, CH
1 NM off per 60 NM flown is 1°
memoryAids: True Virgins Make Dull Company: True, Variation, Magnetic, Deviation, Compass.
East is least, west is best: subtract east variation, add west.
Fly into the wind: wind from the right, heading to the right.
traps: Adding east variation, which gives an answer about twice the variation off.
Applying the wind correction in the wrong direction.
Correcting only the track error and ending up parallel to course.
Using the night 45 minute reserve on a day question, or the reverse.
Forgetting that a reserve is added on top of the trip fuel.

title: The VOR
summary: Read any VOR indication in seconds: which radial you are on, which side of course, and whether the station is ahead or behind.
html:
What a VOR gives you

A VOR transmits 360 magnetic radials, each a course from the station. A VORTAC adds TACAN, which civil airplanes use for DME distance. On the chart, a channel number in the NAVAID box (for example 112.5 Ch 72 PIR) means DME is available.

Identify the station by its Morse code or voice ID before using it. If the ID is missing or the station sends T E S T, it is under maintenance and must not be used, even if the needle looks normal.

Reading the indicator

  • The OBS selects a course. The TO/FROM flag says whether that course takes you toward or away from the station. The CDI shows where that course line is relative to you.
  • Centered needle with FROM: you are on the radial shown on the OBS.
  • Centered needle with TO: you are on the reciprocal radial. OBS 210 TO means you are on the 030 radial, northeast of the station.
  • The indicator ignores heading. Position decides the display, heading only decides whether the needle senses normally.
  • Set the OBS near your heading and the rule is simple: fly toward the needle. Opposite the heading, sensing is reversed.
  • Each dot is about 2°; full deflection is 10° or more. The flag blanks or shows OFF when you are abeam the station relative to the selected course.

Finding a radial on the chart

The compass rose around a VOR is aligned to magnetic north, so read the radial straight off the rose from the station toward the point. Do not use a meridian for this; that would give a true bearing.

Receiver checks

CheckTolerance
VOT (360 FROM or 180 TO)plus or minus 4°
Designated ground checkpointplus or minus 4°
Designated airborne checkpointplus or minus 6°
Dual VOR, same station4° between receivers

The 30 day check and its record (14 CFR 91.171) are required only for IFR.

Service volumes and DME

ClassRange, 1,000 to 12,000 ft AGL
Terminal (T)25 NM
Low altitude (L)40 NM

DME shows slant range. Directly over a station at 6,000 feet above it, DME reads about 1 NM. The error is small once you are at least 1 NM away per 1,000 feet of height.

Fixing position with two VORs

Center each needle with a FROM flag, read both radials, and draw them from their stations. Where they cross is your position.
keyFacts: Magnetic course outbound from the VOR
memoryAids: FROM means you are on what the OBS says; TO means you are on the opposite radial.
VOT: Cessna 182, 360 FROM or 180 TO.
traps: Reading OBS with a TO flag as the radial you are on.
Expecting the indicator to change with heading; it shows position only.
Measuring a radial from a meridian instead of the magnetic compass rose.
Thinking the 30 day VOR check applies to VFR flight.
Expecting DME to read zero directly over the station.

title: GPS, Transponders, ADS-B and Radar Services
summary: Know what GPS integrity monitoring tells you, which transponder code means what, where ADS-B and Mode C are required, and what flight following does and does not do.
html:
GPS

  • A three dimensional fix needs 4 satellites. Integrity monitoring (RAIM) needs 5, or 4 with barometric aiding; excluding a bad satellite needs 6.
  • RAIM warns you when the position may be wrong. When it alerts, switch to pilotage, dead reckoning or VOR right away.
  • Verify every waypoint you enter against the chart. A database can be out of date and a typed waypoint can be wrong.
  • Keep current charts and a flight log; a GPS failure on a VFR flight is a pilotage problem if you have been tracking position.

Transponder codes

CodeMeaning
1200VFR, unless ATC assigns another
7500Unlawful interference
7600Lost communications
7700Emergency

Change codes without passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700. Mode C adds pressure altitude to the reply. Transponders need a test and inspection every 24 calendar months (91.413).

Where Mode C and ADS-B Out are required

  • Class A, B and C airspace, and above the ceiling of Class B or C up to 10,000 feet MSL within their lateral limits.
  • Within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport, surface to 10,000 feet MSL (the Mode C veil).
  • Class E at and above 10,000 feet MSL in the 48 states, except at and below 2,500 feet AGL.

ADS-B In

ADS-B In shows traffic. Only the 978 MHz UAT link also carries FIS-B weather and TFR information. Displayed traffic is an aid; not every aircraft is shown, so keep looking outside.

Radar services for VFR

  • Flight following gives traffic advisories and safety alerts as controller workload permits. You remain responsible for see and avoid, terrain and weather.
  • Request it with call sign, position, altitude and destination, then wait for a code and the words radar contact.
  • Traffic calls use clock positions relative to your ground track. If you are crabbing right, look a little left of the called position.
keyFacts: 30 NM from Class B primary airport, surface to 10,000 MSL
memoryAids: 75 taken alive, 76 radio fix, 77 going to heaven.
Traffic clock is based on track, not nose.
traps: Thinking flight following separates VFR traffic.
Confusing the 24 month transponder check with the 12 month annual.
Expecting FIS-B weather from a 1090 MHz only receiver.
Ignoring a RAIM alert because the moving map still looks normal.

title: The VFR Flight Plan
summary: File, open and close a VFR flight plan correctly, and know exactly when search and rescue starts if you forget.
html:
Why file

A VFR flight plan is optional for most domestic flights. Its value is search and rescue: if you are not heard from, someone starts looking 30 minutes after your ETA.

The form (Figure 51)

ItemEntry
7 Aircraft identificationYour N number
8 Flight rulesV for VFR
Type of flightG for general aviation
9 Type of aircraftICAO type designator, such as C172
10 EquipmentNavigation, communication and surveillance codes
13 Departure aerodrome and timeAirport identifier and proposed time in UTC
15 Cruising speed and levelN0110 for 110 knots; VFR for the level
16 Destination and total EETAirport and estimated time en route
19 EnduranceFuel on board expressed as hours and minutes
19 Persons on boardTotal, including the pilot

Filing, opening, closing

  • File with Flight Service: 1 800 WX BRIEF, the online Flight Service portal, or an EFB that files to it.
  • Open after departure by contacting Flight Service with your departure time. It does not open itself, and the tower does not open it.
  • Close it yourself after landing, even at a towered airport. Towers do not close VFR flight plans.
  • Running late? Call Flight Service and extend the ETA.

Search and rescue timeline

At 30 minutes past ETA without a closure, Flight Service begins communications searches, then alerts search and rescue. A flight plan you forgot to close can launch a real search.
keyFacts: Fuel on board in hours and minutes
Pilot calls Flight Service after departure
memoryAids: File, Open, Close: the pilot does all three.
traps: Believing the tower opens or closes VFR flight plans.
Entering fuel in gallons for endurance.
Thinking search starts one hour after ETA.

title: Diversions, Lost Procedures and Intercepts
summary: Divert early, handle being lost with a clear sequence, and respond correctly if a military aircraft intercepts you.
html:
Diverting

  • Decide early, while weather and fuel still give you choices. Waiting for visibility to drop is how VFR flights end up in clouds.
  • Choose an alternate within range, with suitable runways and better weather. Closeness to the original destination is not the main factor.
  • Turn first using an estimated heading, then refine: distance with the chart scale or a known width, time with groundspeed, fuel with burn rate. Log the time you turned.
  • The pilot in command may divert without permission. Tell ATC or Flight Service and update any flight plan.

When lost

Work through five steps:

  1. Climb, within weather and airspace limits, for better radio and radar coverage and a wider view.
  2. Communicate with ATC or Flight Service, or use 121.5 MHz.
  3. Confess that you are unsure of position.
  4. Comply with the instructions you get.
  5. Conserve fuel with a lower power setting.

Meanwhile hold a steady heading and look for large features such as rivers, highways and railroads. Two VOR radials crossing give a fix. A GPS nearest airport function is a fast check.

If fuel or weather is getting worse, declare an emergency and squawk 7700. Declaring early is the right call. Radar equipped ATC facilities can give vectors to a nearby airport for VFR aircraft in difficulty.

Intercepts

Interceptor signalMeaningYour reply
Rocks wings ahead and to the left, then a slow level turnFollow meRock wings and follow
Abrupt breakaway, climbing turn of 90° or moreYou may proceedRock wings
Circles airport, gear down, overflies runwayLand hereGear down if able, follow, land

Also call on 121.5 MHz, squawk 7700 unless told otherwise, and follow the interceptor's instructions.
keyFacts: Wing rock, then slow level turn
Gear down, low pass over runway
ATC vectors to a nearby airport
memoryAids: The five Cs: climb, communicate, confess, comply, conserve.
traps: Descending low over unfamiliar terrain to read signs.
Waiting to declare an emergency until fuel is critical.
Plotting precisely before turning instead of turning first.
Squawking 7600 instead of 7700 when intercepted.

title: Radio Calls and Phraseology
summary: Say it once, say it right: the format, numbers, and airspace entry rules the test loves.
html:
The shape of every call

An initial call answers four questions in order: who you are calling, who you are, where you are, what you want. Add the ATIS code if there is one. Example: Centerville Tower, Cessna 6413Q, ten miles north, two thousand five hundred, landing, with Bravo. Listen before you transmit, plan the words before you key the mike, and drop old habits like over.

Numbers

ItemExampleSpoken
Altitude below 18,00012,500one two thousand five hundred
Altitude4,500four thousand five hundred
Heading080heading zero eight zero
Frequency118.5one one eight point five
Squawk4231squawk four two three one
Runway31runway three one

Headings always get three digits. Use the ICAO alphabet: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, Xray, Yankee, Zulu. The digit 9 is spoken niner.

Finding frequencies

The Chart Supplement communications section lists CTAF, ATIS, UNICOM, approach, tower, ground, and clearance delivery, with hours. Sectional charts show tower and CTAF frequencies next to the airport. A frequency followed by R means the facility only receives on it; T means it only transmits. RCO listings such as 122.1R with a VOR frequency mean you transmit on 122.1 and listen on the VOR.

Nontowered airports

  • CTAF is the frequency for self announce calls. It may be a UNICOM, the tower frequency when the tower is closed, or MULTICOM 122.9 where there is no tower, FSS, or UNICOM.
  • Inbound: first call about 10 miles out, then entering downwind, base, final, and clear of the runway.
  • Outbound: announce before taxi and before entering the runway.
  • Begin and end each call with the airport name, since many airports share a CTAF.

ATIS

Listen before first contact and report the code. ATIS may omit ceiling, visibility, and obstructions to vision when the ceiling is above 5,000 feet and visibility is more than 5 miles. Wind, altimeter, and runway in use are always there.

Entering controlled airspace

AirspaceEntry requirement
Class BExplicit clearance: cleared into the Class Bravo airspace
Class CTwo way communication: controller answers with your call sign
Class DTwo way communication: controller answers with your call sign

A reply of stand by that includes your call sign establishes communication for C and D. Aircraft calling, stand by does not. Radar contact is never a Class B clearance.

Taxi clearances

Every runway crossing needs an explicit clearance. A taxi instruction to a runway does not authorize crossing other runways on the way. Read back runway assignments, hold short instructions, and crossing clearances.

Emergency frequency

121.5 MHz is the VHF emergency frequency, monitored by FSS, most towers, and many approach facilities. Some towers do not have it, and the Chart Supplement says so in the comm remarks.
