zero eight zero, always three digits
122.9, used where no tower, FSS, or UNICOM exists
Two way communication with your call sign
Facility receives only on that frequency
Each one needs an explicit clearance
memoryAids: Who, who, where, what: the four W call.
B needs a clearance, C and D need my call sign.
traps: Aircraft calling, stand by does not establish communication for Class D.
Radar contact is not a clearance into Class B.
Dropping the leading zero in a heading.
Assuming a taxi to a runway includes crossing other runways.
Treating 122.1R as a two way frequency.

title: Light Signals, Lost Comms, and the ELT
summary: When the radio dies, the tower still talks with colored light. Learn the two columns cold.
html:
ATC light gun signals

14 CFR 91.125 lists the meanings. The same color often means different things on the ground and in the air, so learn the table as two columns.

SignalOn the groundIn flight
Steady greenCleared for takeoffCleared to land
Flashing greenCleared to taxiReturn for landing (steady green to follow)
Steady redStopGive way to other aircraft and continue circling
Flashing redTaxi clear of the runway in useAirport unsafe, do not land
Flashing whiteReturn to starting point on airportNot used
Alternating red and greenExercise extreme cautionExercise extreme caution

Acknowledging

  • In flight, day: rock the wings.
  • In flight, night: flash the landing light or navigation lights.
  • On the ground, day: move the ailerons or rudder.
  • On the ground, night: flash the landing light or navigation lights.

Lost communications arriving VFR at a towered airport

  1. Troubleshoot first: volume, squelch, frequency, headset jacks, push to talk, the avionics master, and circuit breakers.
  2. Squawk 7600.
  3. Stay outside or above the Class D airspace until you see the direction and flow of traffic.
  4. Join the pattern, monitor the tower frequency, and watch the tower for light signals.
  5. Acknowledge signals as above.

If the receiver still works, the tower can talk to you and ask you to acknowledge by turning or flashing lights. If you can transmit but not receive, keep reporting your position; the tower may still hear you.

Emergency locator transmitter

  • ELTs transmit on 121.5 MHz and, in 406 MHz units, on 406 MHz to satellites. Only 406 MHz signals are detected by satellite.
  • Test only during the first 5 minutes after the hour, no more than three audio sweeps.
  • Replace or recharge the battery after more than one cumulative hour of use or when 50 percent of its useful life is gone.
  • Inspect the ELT every 12 calendar months (14 CFR 91.207).
  • After landing, and before shutdown, listen on 121.5 to make sure your ELT has not been activated by a hard landing.
keyFacts: Ground: cleared for takeoff. Air: cleared to land
Ground: cleared to taxi. Air: return for landing
Ground: stop. Air: give way, continue circling
Ground: taxi clear of runway. Air: airport unsafe, do not land
Ground only: return to starting point
First 5 minutes after the hour, three sweeps max
More than 1 cumulative hour of use or 50 percent of life
memoryAids: Steady means the final act (takeoff or land); flashing means the step before it (taxi or come back).
Red flashing on the ground: get off the runway. Red flashing in the air: do not land.
White is only for the ground: go home.
traps: Mixing up steady and flashing green in flight.
Giving the ground meaning of flashing red (taxi clear) for an aircraft in flight.
Rocking the wings at night instead of flashing lights.
Using 12 calendar months as the ELT battery limit; that is the inspection interval.
Squawking 7700 for a simple radio failure.

title: Traffic Patterns and Wind Indicators
summary: Read the wind from the ground, fly the pattern everyone expects, and hold the controls right while you taxi.
html:
The standard pattern

  • Left turns unless right traffic is published (Chart Supplement Rgt tfc, segmented circle indicators, or ATC). This is 14 CFR 91.126.
  • Pattern altitude: use the published TPA, otherwise 1,000 feet AGL for propeller airplanes. Large and turbine aircraft use about 1,500 feet AGL.
  • Entry: on a 45 degree angle to the downwind leg, abeam midfield, level at pattern altitude.
  • Departure: straight out, or a 45 degree turn toward the pattern side beyond the departure end after reaching pattern altitude.

Reading the Chart Supplement TPA

TPA 7470(1000) means 7,470 feet MSL, which is 1,000 feet above the field. The number in parentheses is height above airport elevation. When no TPA is listed, add 1,000 feet to the field elevation.

Wind and landing indicators

IndicatorHow to read it
Wind cone (sock)The tail streams downwind; the wind comes from the end at the pole. A fully extended sock means a strong wind.
TetrahedronThe small pointed end points into the wind, like an airplane nose. It may be free swinging or set by hand.
Landing teeLand toward the crossbar, as if landing on the tee's stem toward its top.
Segmented circleHolds the wind indicator and shows pattern direction with L shaped traffic pattern indicators.

Traffic pattern indicators

Each L shaped indicator sits beside the circle in line with a runway. The long arm is the final approach path and the short arm is the base leg. Picture yourself on final along the long arm: if the base arm sticks out to your right, the pattern is right traffic.

Quartering winds

To name a quartering wind, face the landing direction. Wind from ahead and to one side is a quartering headwind on that side; wind from behind is a quartering tailwind.

Taxi control positions (Figure 9)

WindAileronsElevator, nosewheel airplaneElevator, tailwheel airplane
Left quartering headwindLeft aileron up (turn into wind)NeutralUp
Right quartering headwindRight aileron up (turn into wind)NeutralUp
Left quartering tailwindLeft aileron down (turn away)DownDown
Right quartering tailwindRight aileron down (turn away)DownDown

Noise abatement and local procedures

Read the airport remarks every time. They hold calm wind runways, right traffic, noise sensitive areas, required climb points, glider and parachute activity, and terrain advice, all of which change how you fly the pattern.
keyFacts: 45 degrees to downwind, abeam midfield, at TPA
Wind blows from the pole end toward the tail
Small end points into the wind
Turn into the wind, elevator neutral (nosewheel)
Turn away from the wind, elevator down
memoryAids: Climb into a headwind, dive away from a tailwind.
Tetrahedron: the point points into the wind.
Sit on the long arm of the L: the short arm shows your base turn.
traps: Reading a wind cone's tail direction as the wind direction.
Reading the TPA number in parentheses as MSL.
Forgetting to add field elevation when no TPA is published.
Choosing a closed runway (X at each end) because it lines up with the wind.
Ignoring Rgt tfc on a runway end and flying left traffic.

title: Airport Markings, Signs, and Runway Safety
summary: Yellow means taxiway, white means runway, red means stop: decode every line and sign on the airport.
html:
Colors first

Runway markings are white. Taxiway and holding markings are yellow. Mandatory signs are red with white characters.

Runway markings

  • Displaced threshold: white arrows lead to a white threshold bar. The area before the bar may be used for taxi and takeoff, and for landing rollout from the opposite direction, but not for touchdown.
  • Blast pad or stopway: yellow chevrons. Not for taxi, takeoff, or landing.
  • Closed runway: an X at each end. Not usable at all.
  • Threshold bars, designation numbers, touchdown zone and aiming point markings help you judge where you are on the runway.

Holding position markings

MarkingMeaning
Two solid and two dashed yellow linesRunway holding position. Stop on the solid side unless cleared. Cross freely from the dashed side when leaving the runway.
Same pattern painted on a runwayHold short point for an intersecting runway (used for LAHSO and hold short instructions).
Ladder: two solid lines with cross barsILS critical area holding position.
Single dashed yellow line across a taxiwayTaxiway intersection holding position.
One solid and one dashed line along the edge of a rampNonmovement area boundary.
Continuous double yellow line along a taxiwayTaxiway edge.

After landing, keep taxiing until every part of the airplane is past the holding position marking for the landing runway, then hold unless ATC says otherwise.

Signs

TypeLookExample
Mandatory instructionWhite on red4-22 holding position, ILS, no entry
LocationYellow on black, yellow borderB (you are on taxiway B), 22 (you are on Runway 22)
DirectionBlack on yellow with arrowB with an arrow: taxiway B is that way
DestinationBlack on yellow with arrow22 with an arrow, TERM with an arrow
Runway boundaryYellow with hold line pictureFaces the runway; past it you are clear
ILS critical area boundaryYellow with ladder picturePast it you are clear of the critical area
Runway distance remainingWhite number on black4 means about 4,000 feet left

Runway incursion avoidance

  • Have the airport diagram out and brief the route and hot spots before you taxi.
  • Read back hold short instructions and runway crossings; ask if unsure.
  • Guard against expectation bias when the clearance differs from what you usually get.
  • Look both ways and check the final approach path before entering or crossing any runway.
  • Stop on the solid side of every hold line until you have a clearance.

LAHSO

Land and hold short operations let ATC clear you to land and stop before an intersecting runway, taxiway, or point. The Chart Supplement lists the available distance for each combination. Student pilots and pilots unfamiliar with LAHSO should not participate, and any pilot in command may decline.
keyFacts: Blast pad or stopway: no taxi, takeoff, or landing
Two solid and two dashed; stop on the solid side
Mandatory: hold short of that runway
Yellow sign, black letters with arrow
White number on black beside runway
Students and unfamiliar pilots should decline
memoryAids: Solid side stops you; dashed side lets you go.
Red: required. Black: where I am. Yellow: where I am going.
traps: Thinking the displaced threshold area is unusable for takeoff.
Using a blast pad for takeoff run or landing rollout.
Mistaking a location sign (black) for a destination sign (yellow).
Stopping with the tail still over the hold line after landing.
Reading the LAHSO distance for the wrong runway.

title: Airport and Approach Lighting
summary: From the beacon ten miles out to the PAPI on short final, every light tells you something.
html:
Rotating beacons

AirportBeacon
Lighted civil land airportWhite and green
Military airportDual peaked white flashes between green
Lighted water airportWhite and yellow
HeliportGreen, yellow, and white

Beacons normally run sunset to sunrise. A beacon on in daylight in a Class B, C, D, or E surface area often means the ceiling is below 1,000 feet or visibility below 3 miles. Never rely on it alone; check the weather.

Visual glide slope indicators

Two bar VASI

Far bar over near barPosition
White over whiteAbove glide path
Red over whiteOn glide path
Red over redBelow glide path

VASI provides obstacle clearance within 10 degrees of the extended centerline out to 4 NM.

PAPI (four lights in a row)

LightsPosition
4 whiteWell above
3 white, 1 redSlightly above
2 white, 2 redOn glide path
1 white, 3 redSlightly below
4 redWell below

Tricolor and pulsating systems

Tricolor: amber above, green on path, red below. Pulsating VASI: steady white on path, pulsing white above, steady red slightly below, pulsing red well below.

Runway and taxiway lights

  • Runway edge lights are white. On instrument runways the last 2,000 feet, or half the runway if shorter, show yellow as a caution zone.
  • Threshold lights show green toward an arriving airplane and red toward the end of the runway as seen by a departing airplane.
  • Centerline lights are white, then alternate red and white from 3,000 to 1,000 feet remaining, then all red on the last 1,000 feet.
  • REIL: two synchronized flashing lights at the threshold to help find the runway end.
  • Taxiway edge lights are blue; taxiway centerline lights are green.

Pilot controlled lighting

Clicks within 5 secondsResult
7Highest intensity
5Medium intensity
3Lowest intensity

Always start with seven clicks so every system comes on, then step down. Lights stay on for about 15 minutes after the last activation. The Chart Supplement lists which systems are pilot controlled and the frequency, usually the CTAF. In the airport sketch a negative (white on black) approach light symbol marks pilot controlled lighting.

Reading the codes

LIRL, MIRL, HIRL are low, medium, and high intensity runway lights. MALSR is a medium intensity approach light system with runway alignment indicator lights. P4L means a four light PAPI on the left side; V4L means a four box VASI on the left. GA 3.0 degrees TCH 50 feet gives the glide angle and threshold crossing height.
keyFacts: Yellow edge lights on last 2,000 feet
memoryAids: Red over white, you're all right. White over white, you're high as a kite. Red over red, you're dead.
Blue for the taxiway edge, green to follow the line.
Seven clicks to light the sky, then step down.
traps: Thinking a daytime beacon proves the tower is closed.
Reading three white and one red on a PAPI as slightly low.
Starting with five clicks and missing systems that only respond to seven.
Assuming lights stay on all night when the remarks give a cutoff time.
Confusing P4L (PAPI) with V4L (VASI).

title: Wake Turbulence, Scanning, and Right of Way
summary: The hazards you cannot see and the traffic you fail to see: how to avoid both.
html:
Wingtip vortices

Vortices form whenever a wing makes lift, starting at rotation and ending at touchdown. They are strongest behind an aircraft that is heavy, clean, and slow, because that wing is working at a high angle of attack.

  • They sink, typically a few hundred feet per minute, and level off about 500 to 1,000 feet below the flight path.
  • Near the ground they spread outward at about 2 to 3 knots.
  • A light crosswind can hold the upwind vortex over the runway; a light quartering tailwind can push vortices into the touchdown zone. The light quartering tailwind needs the most caution.
  • Strong winds break vortices up faster.

Avoidance

SituationTechnique
Landing behind a landing large aircraftStay at or above its approach path; land beyond its touchdown point
Landing behind a departing large aircraftLand well before its rotation point
Departing behind a departing large aircraftLift off before its rotation point; climb above or upwind of its path, or wait
Departing behind a landing large aircraftLift off beyond its touchdown point
En route crossing behind a large aircraftStay above its altitude, or well clear

Helicopters also produce strong vortices, especially in forward flight. Avoid hovering and slow moving helicopters by a wide margin.

Scanning for traffic

  • Use short, regularly spaced eye movements, about 10 degrees each, looking at each sector for about 1 second.
  • Traffic on a collision course shows no relative motion; it just grows larger.
  • Clock positions from ATC are based on your ground track, so correct for any crab. Crabbing right, look left of the nose.
  • Clear the area before every turn, and especially before entering the pattern or a runway.
  • At airports with many nonradio aircraft, radio calls do not complete the picture; look harder.

Right of way (14 CFR 91.113)

  • An aircraft in distress has right of way over all others.
  • Converging at about the same altitude: the aircraft on the right has right of way.
  • Head on: both turn right.
  • Overtaking: the overtaken aircraft has right of way; pass to its right.
  • Landing: aircraft on final and landing have right of way over aircraft in flight or on the surface; the lower aircraft has right of way, but do not use that to cut in front of another aircraft.
  • Category order for converging: balloon, glider, airship, then airplane and rotorcraft. An aircraft towing or refueling another has right of way over other engine driven aircraft.
keyFacts: Above its path, land beyond its touchdown
Lift off before its rotation point
Aircraft on the right has right of way
memoryAids: Heavy, clean, slow makes the wake grow.
Over and beyond when they land; before and above when they lift.
traps: Thinking flaps extended make vortices stronger.
Staying below a large aircraft's path to stay out of its way.
Believing strong winds are the worst case for wake turbulence.
Looking straight over the nose for a 12 o'clock call while crabbing.
Pulling onto the runway in front of an aircraft on short final.

title: Using the Chart Supplement
summary: One dense paragraph per airport: learn to pull runway, lighting, comms, and hours out of it in seconds.
html:
The header lines

A typical entry reads LINCOLN (LNK) 4 NW UTC-6(-5DT) ... 1219 B S4 FUEL 100LL, JET A TPA See Remarks.

ItemMeaning
4 NWAirport is 4 NM northwest of the city center
UTC minus 6 (minus 5 DT)Subtract 6 hours from UTC for standard time, 5 for daylight time
1219Field elevation, feet MSL
BRotating beacon, sunset to sunrise unless remarks say otherwise
S4Major airframe and major powerplant repairs
FUEL 100LL100 low lead, blue. Plain 100 is green
OX 1 to OX 4Oxygen service types
TPA 7470(1000)Pattern altitude MSL, then AGL in parentheses
Class I, ARFF Index APart 139 certificated airport and its fire fighting index
AOE or LRAAirport of entry (notice only) or landing rights airport (permission plus notice)

Hours and the double dagger

All times are UTC. A double dagger after a time means the effective hours are one hour earlier during daylight saving time. Example: tower 1200 to 0330Z with a double dagger runs 1100 to 0230Z in summer. To get local time, subtract the UTC offset that applies for the season.

Runway data

  • H7400X100 (ASPH GRVD): hard surface, 7,400 by 100 feet, grooved asphalt. Length includes displaced thresholds but not overruns.
  • S 57, D 95: weight bearing capacity in thousands of pounds for single and dual wheel gear.
  • Lighting: LIRL, MIRL, HIRL, and NSTD for nonstandard systems.
  • Runway end lines carry approach lights, VGSI (for example PAPI(P4R) GA 3.0 degrees TCH 56 feet), displaced thresholds, obstructions, and Rgt tfc.
  • Slope is given when 0.3 percent or more, for example 0.6% up NE.

Declared distances

TermMeaning
TORATakeoff run available
TODATORA plus any clearway
ASDATORA plus any stopway, for accelerate stop
LDARunway available for landing ground roll; reduced by a displaced threshold

Remarks, weather, and communications

  • Airport remarks: attended hours, hazards (birds, deer, gliders), calm wind runway, noise procedures, closed runways, and the ACTIVATE line for pilot controlled lighting.
  • Weather data sources: ASOS, AWOS 1 through 3 with frequency and phone, HIWAS, LLWAS.
  • Communications: CTAF, ATIS, UNICOM, RCO, approach (the circled R means radar), tower with hours, ground, clearance.
  • Airspace: for example Class C svc 1130 to 0600Z double dagger, other times Class E.
  • Comm/Nav/Weather remarks: items such as emergency frequency 121.5 not available at the tower.

The airport sketch

Sketches are oriented to true north. Symbols are in the sketch legend: VASI is a circled V, PAPI a circled P, approach lights a circled A with a number, and a negative symbol means pilot controlled. Closed runways are shown with X marks at each end.

Hours one hour earlier during daylight saving time
Major airframe and major powerplant repairs
memoryAids: Double dagger, daylight: one hour earlier.
Header tells what the airport has; remarks tell what can bite you.
traps: Forgetting the double dagger shift for summer hours.
Using the standard time offset in summer.
Reading 100 as 100LL.

Confusing AOE with LRA.

title: The Body at Altitude
summary: Hypoxia hides its own symptoms, and most aeromedical test items come down to recognizing the type and knowing the fix.
html:
Four kinds of hypoxia

TypeWhat failsTypical cause
HypoxicNot enough oxygen pressure in the airAltitude
Hypemic (anemic)Blood cannot carry enough oxygenCarbon monoxide, blood donation, anemia
StagnantBlood does not circulate wellHigh G loads, shock, cold extremities
HistotoxicCells cannot use the oxygenAlcohol, some drugs, poisons

Early symptoms include euphoria, a false sense of well being, headache, slowed reactions, poor judgment, and dimmer vision, then cyanosis and drowsiness. The danger is that the affected pilot rarely notices. The fix is oxygen or a descent.

Oxygen: AIM advice versus the rule

The AIM recommends supplemental oxygen above 10,000 feet cabin altitude by day and above 5,000 feet at night. The regulation (14 CFR 91.211) is a separate, higher legal floor. Know which one a question is asking about.

Hyperventilation

Breathing too fast and deep, usually from stress or anxiety, blows off carbon dioxide. Symptoms are lightheadedness, tingling, muscle spasms, and a feeling of suffocation, which overlap with hypoxia. Fix: slow the breathing rate, breathe into a bag, or talk aloud. If you are using oxygen, first confirm the oxygen system is working.

Ears and sinuses

The Eustachian tube vents air out of the middle ear easily on the climb but resists air flowing back in on the descent, so ear block shows up during descent. Equalize by swallowing, yawning, or the Valsalva maneuver. Do not fly with a cold or sinus congestion; a block can cause severe pain and damage.

Carbon monoxide

Colorless and odorless, usually from a leaking exhaust heater muff. Symptoms: headache, drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision. Fix: heater off, fresh air vents open, oxygen if available, land. Susceptibility rises with altitude, so climbing makes it worse.

Scuba diving (AIM guidance)

DiveFlight altitudeWait
No controlled ascentUp to 8,000 ft MSL12 hours
No controlled ascentAbove 8,000 ft MSL24 hours
Required a controlled ascentAny altitude24 hours

Oxygen does not solve this problem; the nitrogen is already in the blood.

Medications and alcohol

Over the counter drugs such as antihistamines, cold remedies, and sleep aids can cause drowsiness and impair judgment, and the condition being treated may itself be disqualifying. Safest rule: do not fly while taking any medication unless the FAA has approved it. The alcohol rule of 14 CFR 91.17 (8 hours, 0.04) does not make a sedating drug safe.

IMSAFE

Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion. Look at the combined picture, not one item at a time.

Alcohol or drugs; cells cannot use oxygen
Poor circulation, such as high G
Above 10,000 ft by day, above 5,000 ft at night
Slow breathing, breathe into a bag, talk aloud
12 hours up to 8,000 ft; 24 hours above

Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion

Scuba: 12 low, 24 high, 24 always after a controlled ascent.
traps: Confusing the AIM oxygen recommendation (10,000 day, 5,000 night) with the 12,500 foot rule of 91.211.
Picking the 12 hour scuba wait when the dive needed a controlled ascent or the flight goes above 8,000 feet.

Calling carbon monoxide poisoning hypoxic hypoxia; it is hypemic.
Climbing to clear carbon monoxide symptoms; altitude makes it worse.

title: Spatial Disorientation and Visual Illusions
summary: Your inner ear lies whenever you lose the horizon, and runway shapes lie on every unfamiliar approach.
html:
Why the inner ear fails

The semicircular canals sense rotation only while it is changing; after about 20 seconds of a steady turn the fluid catches up and the turn is no longer felt. The otolith organs cannot tell acceleration from tilt. Without a visual horizon the brain trusts these signals, and they are often wrong. The defense is always the same: believe the instruments.

Vestibular illusions

IllusionCauseFalse sensation and danger
The leansAbrupt roll out after an unnoticed slow bankFeels banked the other way; pilot rolls back into the bank
CoriolisAbrupt head movement in a prolonged turnRotation in a totally different axis; overwhelming
Graveyard spiralProlonged turn feels level; altitude loss noticedPilot pulls back with wings banked, tightening the spiral
Graveyard spinRecovery from a spin feels like a spin the other wayPilot reenters the original spin
SomatogravicRapid acceleration, as on takeoffFeels nose up; pushing over flies into terrain
InversionAbrupt change from climb to levelFeels like tumbling backward; pilot pitches down
ElevatorUpdraft or downdraftUpdraft feels like a climb, invites nose down

Graveyard spiral recovery: level the wings on the attitude indicator first, then raise the nose. Back pressure in a bank only tightens the turn.

Visual illusions on approach

ConditionYou feelResulting approach
Narrower runway than usualHigherToo low
Wider runway than usualLowerToo high
Upsloping runway or terrainHigherToo low
Downsloping runwayLowerToo high
Featureless terrain, water, snow (black hole at night)HigherToo low
Rain on the windshield (water refraction)HigherToo low
HazeFarther away and higherToo low

Other visual traps: flying into fog can create the illusion of pitching up, so the pilot may steepen the approach abruptly. Water refraction from rain on the windshield makes the horizon appear lower, leading to a low approach. Bright runway and approach lights, especially where few lights illuminate the surrounding terrain, make the runway seem closer than it is, so the pilot may fly a higher approach. Overflying terrain with few lights to give height cues tends to produce a lower than normal approach. Use a VASI or PAPI whenever available, and fly the same pattern and glidepath every time.

Inadvertent IMC

Trust the attitude indicator, keep the wings level, make a gentle turn of no more than standard rate back to where the weather was VMC, use the autopilot if you have one, and ask ATC for help.
keyFacts: Abrupt correction of an unnoticed bank feels like the opposite bank
Head movement in a prolonged turn; most overwhelming
Level the wings first, then raise the nose
Acceleration feels like nose up; risk of pushing over
Climb to level abruptly feels like tumbling backward
memoryAids: Most visual illusions make you feel high and fly low. Only wide and downsloping runways make you feel low.
Rolling out of a spiral: wings first, nose second.
traps: Reversing the narrow and wide runway effects.
Calling an abrupt head movement in a turn the leans; it is Coriolis.

title: Night Vision and Night Flying
summary: At night you see with the edges of your eyes, read other airplanes by their light colors, and legally carry passengers only after full stop landings.
html:
How the eye works at night

  • Cones sit in the center (fovea), see color and detail, and need good light.
  • Rods surround the center, work in dim light, and detect motion, but see no color or detail.
  • Because the fovea has no rods, there is a night blind spot straight ahead. Use off center viewing: look 5 to 10 degrees to the side of an object.
  • Each eye also has a fixed blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina; the other eye normally covers it, so keep scanning.

Dark adaptation

About 30 minutes in darkness for full adaptation. A glance at a bright light undoes much of it in seconds; close one eye to protect it. Use dim cockpit lighting. Smoking, carbon monoxide, and altitude (from about 5,000 feet) reduce night vision; the AIM recommends oxygen above 5,000 feet at night.

Night illusions

  • Autokinesis: a stationary light stared at seems to move. Keep the eyes moving.
  • False horizon: sloping clouds, shorelines, or ground lights mixed with stars mistaken for the horizon. Cross check the attitude indicator.
  • Empty field myopia: with nothing to focus on, the eyes focus close by. Focus on distant lights.
  • Black hole approach: dark terrain before a lit runway makes you feel high, so you fly too low.

Required lights and equipment

Night VFR (14 CFR 91.205(c)) adds to the day VFR list: approved position lights, an approved anticollision light system, an adequate source of electrical energy, and one spare set of fuses (or three of each kind) accessible in flight if the airplane uses fuses. A landing light is required only for hire. Lights must be on from sunset to sunrise (14 CFR 91.209). Carry a flashlight, preferably with a red or white option.

Reading other airplanes' lights

You seeMeaning
Red only, with white strobe or beaconYou see its left side; it moves from your right to your left
Green onlyYou see its right side; it moves from your left to your right
Green on the left and red on the rightIt is coming toward you
White steady light onlyYou see its tail; it is moving away

Red left, green right, white tail. A light holding a constant position on your windshield means a collision course. An airplane on your right has the right of way.

Airport lighting in brief

Rotating beacon: white and green for a civil land airport. Runway edge lights white (yellow on the last 2,000 feet of instrument runways), threshold green from the approach side, runway end red, taxiway edge lights blue, taxiway centerline green. Pilot controlled lighting: key the mic 7 times for high intensity, 5 for medium, 3 for low, all within 5 seconds.

Night currency

To carry passengers at night (14 CFR 61.57(b)): 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop, in the same category and class (and type if required), within the preceding 90 days, during the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. Touch and go landings do not count. Currency is the legal minimum, not proficiency.

Left wingtip; traffic moving right to left
Right wingtip; traffic moving left to right
Position lights, anticollision lights, electrical source, spare fuses
3 full stop landings, 1 hr after sunset to 1 hr before sunrise, 90 days
7 clicks high, 5 medium, 3 low, within 5 seconds
memoryAids: Red left, green right, white tail.
Rods for the rim, cones for the center.
traps: Counting touch and go landings toward night passenger currency.
Using the 1996 anticollision date rule to skip anticollision lights at night.
Staring straight at a dim light instead of looking slightly off to the side.
Thinking a landing light is required for all night VFR flights.

title: Decision Making and Hazardous Attitudes
summary: Most accidents start with a decision, and the FAA gives you a handful of models to make better ones.
html:
The five hazardous attitudes

AttitudeSounds likeAntidote
AntiauthorityDo not tell me what to doFollow the rules. They are usually right.
ImpulsivityDo something, quicklyNot so fast. Think first.
InvulnerabilityIt will not happen to meIt could happen to me.
MachoI can do it; watch thisTaking chances is foolish.
ResignationWhat is the use?I am not helpless. I can make a difference.

Risk management models

  • PAVE (identify hazards): Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures.
  • IMSAFE (inside the P): Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.
  • 3P: Perceive the hazard (PAVE), Process it (CARE: Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors), Perform (TEAM: Transfer, Eliminate, Accept, Mitigate).
  • DECIDE: Detect the change, Estimate the need to react, Choose an outcome, Identify actions, Do the action, Evaluate the effect.

Single pilot resource management

SRM is using every resource available: ATC, Flight Service, passengers (to watch for traffic or hold a chart), checklists, and automation. Its skills include task management (aviate, navigate, communicate, and doing tasks early in low workload phases), situational awareness (knowing where you are, what the airplane is doing, and what is coming next), and automation management (always knowing the active and armed modes, and hand flying when the automation does not do what you expect).

Stress and fatigue

Acute stress is the immediate reaction to a threat; chronic stress is a continuing load beyond your ability to cope and is a reason not to fly. Acute fatigue is short term and relieved by rest; chronic fatigue builds over days and needs prolonged rest.

Personal minimums

Set on the ground, in writing, above the legal minimums, covering ceiling, visibility, wind, crosswind, night, and recent experience. Their value is that you do not renegotiate them under pressure. Get home pressure, waiting passengers, and sunk cost are the classic external pressures. Checklists protect against memory lapses under stress.
keyFacts: Follow the rules. They are usually right.
I am not helpless. I can make a difference.
Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
memoryAids: 3P uses PAVE to perceive, CARE to process, TEAM to perform.
The E in PAVE is External pressures; the V is enVironment.
traps: Taking the E in PAVE to mean environment or emotion.
Matching the macho antidote to antiauthority, or the reverse.
Putting DECIDE inside the 3P model; it is a separate model.
Assuming legal weather means the flight fits your personal minimums.

title: Emergency Procedures
summary: Fly the airplane first, then the checklist, then the radio, and know the few numbers the test always asks.
html:
Engine failure in flight

  1. Pitch for best glide at once and trim.
  2. Pick a field, preferably into the wind, within easy gliding distance.
  3. Run the restart checklist: fuel selector, mixture, carburetor heat, magnetos, fuel pump, primer locked.
  4. Communicate: 7700, 121.5 MHz or the frequency in use, position and intentions.
  5. Secure the engine and brief passengers before landing.

Best glide versus minimum sink

Best glide gives the most distance per foot of altitude (best lift to drag). Minimum sink is slower and gives the most time aloft, but less distance. Best glide speed decreases as weight decreases, but the glide distance stays about the same. A headwind shortens and a tailwind lengthens the glide over the ground. Hold a constant glide speed; changing it ruins the judgment of where you will land.

Low altitude failure after takeoff

Lower the nose immediately and land generally straight ahead with only small heading changes. The turn back to the runway takes far more altitude than pilots expect and is a classic stall spin trap.

Partial power loss

Often more dangerous than a total failure because of the temptation to keep going or let the airspeed decay. Fly, troubleshoot, head for a landing site, and plan for a complete failure.

Fire

FireFirst actions (typical POH)
Engine fire in flightMixture idle cutoff, fuel selector off, master off, cabin heat and air off; do not restart; emergency descent and forced landing
Electrical fireMaster off, vents and cabin heat closed, extinguisher if needed, then restore only essential circuits if the POH allows

The smell of burning insulation is the classic first sign of an electrical fire.

Emergency descent

Used for fire, smoke, or a medical emergency. Power idle, configure per the POH, and bank 30 to 45 degrees to keep a positive load factor while descending. Stay within VNE, VFE, and VLE, and use a lower speed if structural damage is suspected.

Door open in flight

Noisy but rarely dangerous. Fly the airplane, return for a normal landing, close it on the ground. The startle response is the real hazard.

Codes, radio, and ELT

ItemValue
Emergency7700
Lost communications7600
Hijacking7500
Emergency frequency121.5 MHz
ELT test windowFirst 5 minutes after the hour, no more than 3 audio sweeps
ELT batteryReplace or recharge after 1 cumulative hour of use or 50 percent of useful life
ELT inspectionEvery 12 calendar months

Declare early. Under 14 CFR 91.3 the pilot in command may deviate from any rule to the extent needed to meet an emergency, and must send a written report if the FAA requests it.

Survival gear

Plan to survive 48 to 72 hours: water, clothing, and shelter first. In the cold, protecting body heat comes before water and food. Over water, carry flotation; over mountains, carry signaling and warmth.

title: Takeoff and Landing Techniques
summary: Each takeoff and landing variant exists to solve one problem; know the problem and the technique follows.
html:
Speeds

  • VX: best angle of climb, most altitude per distance. Use to clear obstacles.
  • VY: best rate of climb, most altitude per time. Normal climb after obstacles are cleared.

Crosswind

Takeoff: full aileron into the wind at the start of the roll, reduced as speed builds; rudder keeps the centerline. After liftoff, turn into the wind to crab. Landing: crab on final, then the wing low (sideslip) method in the flare, aileron into the wind and opposite rudder to align the nose. The upwind main wheel touches first, and aileron into the wind increases as the airplane slows.

Soft field

Problem: mud, grass, or snow drag on the wheels and the nose wheel. Keep moving, hold back pressure to lighten the nose wheel, lift off at the lowest possible speed, then lower the nose slightly and accelerate in ground effect to VX or VY before climbing. Land with a little power, at minimum sink rate, and keep the nose wheel off as long as possible.

Ground effect

Within about one wingspan of the surface, wingtip vortices and downwash are reduced, so induced drag drops. An airplane can lift off too slowly to climb out of ground effect, and excess speed in the flare causes floating.

Short field

Takeoff: use all the runway, brakes held while setting full power, rotate at the POH speed, climb at VX or the obstacle clearance speed until clear, then VY. Landing: stabilized approach at the POH speed, or no more than 1.3 VSO if none is published; touch down at the point with little float; ACS tolerance is 200 feet beyond the point. Excess speed means float.

Forward slip

Steepens the descent without increasing airspeed, using drag from the side of the fuselage. Check the POH for slip limits with flaps; airspeed indications may be in error while slipping. Straighten out before touchdown.

Go around

Decide early. Full power, expect a strong nose up tendency with nose up trim, hold forward pressure, pitch for VX or VY, retract flaps in stages once climbing, retrim, and move to the side of the runway if needed to see traffic.

TaskACS touchdown tolerance
Normal and crosswind landingWithin 400 feet beyond the point
Short field landingWithin 200 feet beyond the point
Forward slip to a landingWithin 400 feet beyond the point

traps: Using VY instead of VX to clear an obstacle.

title: Ground Reference Maneuvers and Steep Turns
summary: Groundspeed sets bank: fastest over the ground means steepest bank, and crab is biggest when the wind is straight across.
html:
The one rule

To fly a constant radius over the ground, bank angle must follow groundspeed. Downwind, groundspeed is highest, so bank is steepest. Upwind, groundspeed is lowest, so bank is shallowest. Crab angle is largest when the wind is directly across the track, and zero with a direct headwind or tailwind.

Rectangular course (Figure 62)

In Figure 62 the wind blows from the top of the figure toward the bottom and the airplane flies counterclockwise with left turns: 1 to 2 crosswind (wind from the right), 2 to 3 downwind, 3 to 4 crosswind (wind from the left), 4 to 1 upwind.

CornerEntering fromBankHeading change
1Upwind legShallow, increasingLess than 90 degrees
2Crosswind legMedium, increasing to steepMore than 90 degrees
3Downwind legSteep, decreasingMore than 90 degrees
4Crosswind legMedium, decreasing to shallowLess than 90 degrees

The rectangular course models the traffic pattern: upwind leg as final, the 2 to 3 leg as downwind, and the 3 to 4 leg as base. The ACS has you enter at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, 45 degrees to the downwind leg.

S turns (Figure 66)

In Figure 66 the wind blows from the bottom of the figure toward the top. The airplane crosses the road heading downwind at 1, turns right through 2 to cross the road heading upwind at 3 and 4, then turns left through 5 to cross heading downwind at 6.

PositionSituationBankCrab
1 and 6Heading downwindSteepestNone
2 and 5CrosswindMedium, changingLargest, nose toward the bottom of the figure (into the wind)
3 and 4Heading upwindShallowest, wings level crossing the roadNone

Downwind half circle: steep to shallow. Upwind half circle: shallow to steep. A constant bank lets the wind distort the half circles.

Steep turns

ACS: 45 degree bank, 360 degrees, entry altitude within 100 feet, airspeed within 10 knots, bank within 5 degrees, roll out within 10 degrees of the entry heading, entry speed at or below VA. Load factor at 45 degrees is about 1.41 G, and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, about 19 percent. Above about 30 degrees of bank, overbanking tendency appears and needs slight opposite aileron. VA decreases as weight decreases.
keyFacts: Start of corner 3, out of the downwind leg
Steep turn load factor at 45 degrees
memoryAids: Fast over the ground, steep in the turn.
Crab is greatest when the wind is on your wing.
traps: Placing the steepest bank where the airplane heads into the wind.
Thinking every rectangular course corner is a 90 degree heading change.
Putting the largest crab at the downwind or upwind crossing of an S turn.
Assuming the gross weight VA protects a lightly loaded airplane.

title: Slow Flight, Stalls, Spins, and Unusual Attitudes
summary: A wing stalls at one angle of attack, not one airspeed, and every recovery starts by reducing it.
html:
Angle of attack is the whole story

Angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the relative wind (angle A in Figure 1). A wing stalls when it exceeds its critical angle of attack, at any airspeed, attitude, or weight. Stall speed rises with load factor and weight; it falls with lower weight and flaps.

Slow flight

To hold altitude while slowing, the angle of attack must increase. Below the speed for minimum drag, the airplane is on the back side of the power curve, the region of reversed command, where flying slower needs more power. Controls feel mushy, left turning tendencies are stronger, and right rudder is needed with high power.

Stalls

  • Power off stalls simulate approach and landing; power on stalls simulate takeoff and departure climb.
  • Recovery: reduce the angle of attack first, level the wings with coordinated controls, add power as needed, then return to the desired flightpath.
  • Secondary stall: pulling back too abruptly during recovery.
  • Accelerated stall: stall above the normal stall speed due to high load factor, as in a steep turn.
  • Cross control stall: skidding turn, often base to final, with rudder into the turn and opposite aileron; the inside wing stalls first and the airplane rolls into the turn toward a spin.
  • Elevator trim stall: full power on a go around with nose up trim pitches the nose up sharply.

Spins

A spin needs two things: a stall and yaw, which leaves one wing more deeply stalled than the other. Phases are entry, incipient, developed, and recovery. Standard recovery unless the POH says otherwise:

  1. Power to idle.
  2. Ailerons neutral.
  3. Full rudder opposite the rotation.
  4. Brisk forward elevator to break the stall.
  5. Neutralize rudder when rotation stops, then recover from the dive smoothly.

Unusual attitude recovery by instruments

AttitudeRecovery order
Nose high, airspeed decreasingAdd power, lower the nose, level the wings
Nose low, airspeed increasingReduce power, level the wings, raise the nose smoothly

Basic attitude instrument flying uses the attitude indicator as the center of the scan, with radial cross checks to the other instruments. Avoid fixation on one instrument and omission of others. In inadvertent IMC, trust the instruments, make a gentle turn back to VMC, and ask ATC for help.
keyFacts: At the critical angle of attack, any airspeed
Back side of the power curve
Pulling back too soon during recovery
Skid; inside wing stalls; rolls into the turn
Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite, Elevator forward
Power off, wings level, then nose up
Power on, nose down, then wings level
memoryAids: PARE: Power, Ailerons, Rudder, Elevator.
Nose low: wings before nose. Nose high: nose before wings.
traps: Thinking a stall happens at one fixed airspeed.
Using aileron to pick up a dropping wing in a stall or spin.
Raising the nose before leveling the wings in a nose low spiral.
Tightening an overshooting base to final turn with rudder instead of going around.

title: 152 Engine, Fuel and Electrical
summary: How the 152 makes power, feeds fuel, makes electricity and drives its instruments.
html:
Numbers here come from the 1978 Model 152 POH. Other model years and printings differ in a few places. The POH and the weight and balance sheet kept in the club airplane are the documents that govern; check them before you fly.

Engine and propeller

Lycoming O-235-L2C: four cylinders, horizontally opposed, air cooled, carbureted, 110 hp at 2550 RPM, wet sump. A fixed pitch two blade McCauley propeller, 69 inches in diameter, turns at engine speed, so the tachometer is your only power gauge. The tachometer is mechanical and the hour meter in it logs engine time.

Two magnetos, two plugs per cylinder. Each magneto serves one top and one bottom plug on opposite sides: the right magneto handles the upper left and lower right plugs, the left magneto the upper right and lower left. The ignition switch reads OFF, R, L, BOTH, START. Magnetos make their own spark, so the engine keeps running with the master off, and a broken ground wire means a live propeller even with the key off.

Induction and carburetor

Ram air enters through a filter in the lower cowling into an airbox and then the updraft, float type carburetor under the engine. Carburetor heat opens a valve in the airbox to hot, unfiltered air from a shroud around the muffler. Full heat at full throttle costs about 150 to 200 RPM. Keep it off on the ground unless needed. The carburetor has no accelerator pump, so pumping the throttle when starting does nothing useful. A manual primer pulls fuel from the strainer and squirts it into the intake ports; lock it after use, because an unlocked primer can upset the mixture and make the engine run rough.

Oil

Sump capacity 6 quarts, plus 1 if a full flow filter is installed. Never fly with less than 4 quarts. Fill to 5 for flights under three hours and to 6 for long flights; above that the extra oil mostly goes out the breather. Normal oil pressure is 60 to 90 psi, minimum 25 at idle, max 100 (1978 book). Oil temperature green arc 100 to 245 F.

Fuel

  • Two wing tanks feed by gravity through one ON/OFF shutoff valve and a strainer to the carburetor. No pump, no LEFT/RIGHT/BOTH selector.
  • Venting: a line connects the right tank to the left; the left tank vents overboard through a tube with a check valve under the left wing near the strut. The right filler cap is vented too. A blocked vent cuts fuel flow and can stop the engine, so look at that tube every preflight.
  • Standard tanks hold 13 gallons each, 24.5 usable total. About 0.75 gallon per tank remains when the gauge shows E. The gauges are electric float types and unreliable in slips and skids.
  • Because fuel crossfeeds between tanks, top off again after fueling to really get full tanks.
  • Sample both tank sumps and pull the strainer drain for about four seconds before the first flight of the day and after each fueling. If you find water, keep draining until it is clear.

Electrical

28 volt DC system: a 60 amp belt driven alternator and a 24 volt battery on the right forward side of the firewall. The split master has BAT (right half, all electrical power) and ALT (left half, the alternator). The ammeter shows charge into or discharge out of the battery. If the alternator quits or the load exceeds its output, the needle shows discharge.

Over voltage protection (1978 book): a sensor shuts the alternator down at about 31.5 volts and turns on a red HIGH VOLTAGE light. Reset by turning both halves of the master off and on. Later 152s use a low voltage warning light and a different checklist; know which one your club airplane has.

Not on the master: the ignition, the clock and the hour recorder. Most circuits use push to reset breakers. For a light that fails, the POH allows one reset of a popped breaker if there is no sign of a short; if it pops again, leave it out. The wing flaps are electric (15 amp FLAP breaker), so a dead electrical system means a no flap landing.

Flight instruments

SourceInstruments
Pitot tube (left wing) and static port (left side of the fuselage)Airspeed, altimeter, vertical speed
Engine driven vacuum pumpAttitude indicator, directional indicator; suction gauge 4.6 to 5.4 in. Hg
ElectricalTurn coordinator, fuel gauges, oil temperature
Direct oil pressure lineOil pressure gauge

Stall warning is pneumatic: an inlet in the left wing leading edge and a reed horn near the upper left corner of the windshield. It needs no electrical power. Test it on preflight by covering the opening with a clean cloth and gently applying suction.

Other bits worth knowing

  • Nose wheel steering through the rudder pedals covers about 8.5 degrees each side; differential braking adds up to 30 degrees. Never tow with more than 30 degrees of nose wheel turn.
  • Brakes are hydraulic discs on the mains, toe operated. Spongy pedals: pump them. One brake fails: use the other sparingly with opposite rudder.
  • If a door pops open in flight you do not need to land. Trim for about 65 knots, push the door out slightly and then pull it firmly shut.
  • The elevator trim wheel turns forward for nose down and aft for nose up.

title: 152 Normal Procedures Flow
summary: Preflight to tie down in the order the POH flies it, with the speeds that go with each step.
html:
Numbers here come from the 1978 Model 152 POH. Other model years and printings differ in a few places. The POH and the weight and balance sheet kept in the club airplane are the documents that govern; check them before you fly.

Preflight walkaround

  1. Cabin: control lock out, ignition OFF, master ON to read the fuel gauges (and test lights or pitot heat), master OFF, fuel valve ON.
  2. Empennage: rudder gust lock off, tail tiedown off, surfaces free and secure.
  3. Right wing: aileron, tiedown, tire, sump sample, fuel visually checked, cap secure.
  4. Nose: oil at least 4 quarts, strainer drain about four seconds, propeller and spinner for nicks, air filter clear, landing light, nose strut and tire, tiedown, static port on the left side clear.
  5. Left wing: tire, sump sample, fuel, cap, pitot cover off, stall warning inlet and fuel vent clear, tiedown, aileron.

Remove even a thin layer of frost before flight. For a night flight, check every light and carry a flashlight.

Start (above freezing)

Mixture RICH, carb heat COLD, prime up to 3 strokes as needed (one is usually enough when warm), throttle open about 1/2 inch, propeller area clear, master ON, ignition START, then 1000 RPM or less. Oil pressure must show within 30 seconds in summer, about 60 seconds in very cold weather, or shut down. Black smoke and weak firing mean flooding: mixture idle cutoff, full throttle, crank, then start again without priming.

Before takeoff

  • Parking brake set, doors latched, controls free and correct, instruments set, fuel ON, mixture RICH (below 3000 ft), trim to takeoff.
  • Throttle 1700 RPM: magnetos (drop no more than 125 RPM, difference no more than 50), carb heat (RPM drop), engine instruments and ammeter, suction.
  • No drop at all on a magneto may mean a broken ground wire: a hot magneto.
  • For night flight, load the system with the landing light or flaps during the runup; the ammeter should stay within one needle width.

Takeoff and climb

PhaseConfiguration and speed
Normal takeoffFlaps 0 to 10, full throttle, lift the nose wheel at 50 KIAS, climb 65 to 75
Short fieldFlaps 10, full power on the brakes, slightly tail low, 54 KIAS to clear obstacles, retract flaps slowly after 60
Soft fieldFlaps 10, lift off as soon as practical tail low, level off in ground effect to accelerate
CrosswindMinimum flaps for the field, accelerate a little faster, lift off firmly, then correct for drift
Enroute climb70 to 80 KIAS, full throttle, lean above 3000 ft for max RPM
Best rate or angleVY 67 at sea level (61 at 10,000), VX 55

Flaps beyond 10 degrees are not approved for takeoff. Check during the takeoff roll that the full throttle RPM is about 2280 to 2380; a rough or sluggish engine is reason to abort. Above 3000 ft field elevation, lean for max RPM before takeoff.

Cruise

Normal cruise is 55 to 75 percent power, 1900 to 2550 RPM. Lean until RPM peaks and drops 25 to 50 RPM. An unexplained RPM loss means carburetor ice: full heat, then find the minimum heat that keeps it away. Use full carb heat in very heavy rain.

Approach and landing

ApproachSpeed
Normal, flaps up60 to 70 KIAS
Normal, flaps 3055 to 65 KIAS
Short field, flaps 3054 KIAS; idle once the obstacle is cleared; mains first; retract flaps, full up elevator and heavy braking
Go aroundFull throttle, carb heat COLD, flaps to 20, 55 KIAS, then the rest of the flaps up slowly

Before landing: seats and belts, mixture RICH, carb heat ON before you reduce power. Flaps only below 85 KIAS. In a strong crosswind use the minimum flaps for the field. Touch down on the mains with power off and lower the nose wheel gently.

After landing and securing

Flaps up, carb heat cold. Securing: parking brake, radios off, mixture idle cutoff, ignition OFF, master OFF, control lock in.

title: 152 Emergency Procedures
summary: The memory items, the speeds that go with them, and why each step is there.
html:
Numbers here come from the 1978 Model 152 POH. Other model years and printings differ in a few places. The POH and the weight and balance sheet kept in the club airplane are the documents that govern; check them before you fly.

Emergency airspeeds (KIAS)

SituationSpeed
Engine failure after takeoff60
Best glide60
Forced landing, flaps up65
Forced landing, flaps down60
Precautionary landing with power55 on final (flaps 30)
Engine fire in flight85, faster if the fire persists
Iced approach65 to 75, flaps up
Maneuvering104, 98, 93 at 1670, 1500, 1350 lb

Engine failures

During the takeoff roll: throttle idle, brakes, flaps up, mixture idle cutoff, ignition off, master off. Stopping on the runway is the whole job.

Right after takeoff: lower the nose at once to 60 KIAS, then mixture idle cutoff, fuel valve off, ignition off, flaps as needed, master off. Land nearly straight ahead with only small turns. The POH says altitude and airspeed are seldom enough to turn back to the runway.

In flight (restart): 60 KIAS, then carb heat ON, primer IN and LOCKED, fuel valve ON, mixture RICH, ignition BOTH (START if the propeller has stopped). Think of it as checking the causes in order: ice, primer, fuel, mixture, spark.

Glide: the POH chart is a straight line of 1.6 nm per 1000 ft above the terrain at 60 KIAS, flaps up, propeller windmilling. From 3000 ft AGL that is about 4.8 nm; from 5000 ft, 8 nm. A headwind shortens it, and slowing below 60 shortens it too.

Forced and precautionary landings

  • Without power: 65 flaps up or 60 flaps down, mixture idle cutoff, fuel valve off, ignition off, flaps as needed (30 recommended), master off, doors unlatched before touchdown, touch down slightly tail low, brake hard.
  • With power: 60 KIAS and flaps 20 to fly over the field and look at it, climb out and retract the flaps, radios and electrical off, flaps 30 on final at 55, master off, doors unlatched, ignition off, brake hard.
  • Ditching: Mayday on 121.5, secure or toss heavy items, land into the wind in high wind or along the swells in light wind, flaps 30, 300 fpm descent at 55, doors unlatched, level touchdown, cushion your face.

Fires

FireFirst moves
On the ground during startKeep cranking to suck the fire into the engine; if it starts, run 1700 RPM briefly, then shut down and inspect. If not: keep cranking, get an extinguisher, master, ignition and fuel off, put it out.
Engine fire in flightMixture idle cutoff, fuel valve off, master off, cabin heat and air off (wing root vents may stay open), 85 KIAS, forced landing. No restart.
Electrical fireMaster off, all switches off except ignition, vents and heat closed, extinguisher. If power is needed: master on, do not reset popped breakers, add equipment one item at a time.
Cabin fireMaster off, vents and heat closed, extinguisher, land as soon as possible. Ventilate after using an extinguisher.
Wing fireNav, strobe and pitot heat off; slip to keep flames away from the tank and cabin; land with flaps up.

The first sign of an electrical fire is usually the smell of hot insulation.

Electrical problems

  • HIGH VOLTAGE light (1978): master off (both halves), master on. If the light comes back, the alternator is down for good: end the flight as soon as practical and save the battery for flaps and landing light.
  • Ammeter shows discharge: alternator off, nonessential equipment off, end the flight as soon as practical.
  • After 30 minutes of cruise the charge should be under two needle widths; a higher rate means overcharging.
  • Later 152s have a low voltage light with its own checklist. Know your club airplane's version.

Rough engine and oil

  • Gradual RPM loss then roughness: carb ice. Full throttle and full heat until it runs smoothly.
  • Slight roughness: probably fouled plugs. Check on L and R, lean to cruise setting, then try richer.
  • Sudden roughness: probably a magneto. Find the bad one, try power and mixture, fly on the good one if you must.
  • Low oil pressure, normal temperature: may be the gauge or relief valve; land at the nearest airport.
  • Low oil pressure and rising temperature: engine failure is near. Reduce power and set up a forced landing.

Icing, vacuum failure and spins

Icing: pitot heat on if installed, turn back or change altitude, cabin heat full for defrost, more RPM to shed propeller ice, carb heat as needed. Plan the nearest airport, keep flaps up, approach at 65 to 75, use a forward slip for visibility, land level.

Vacuum failure in cloud: attitude and heading indicators are lost; fly the electric turn coordinator. For a 180, make a standard rate turn for 60 seconds. For a descent, use full rich, full carb heat, 500 to 800 fpm, trim 70 KIAS, hands off, steer with rudder.

Spin recovery: ailerons neutral, throttle idle, full opposite rudder, then brisk forward elevator just after the rudder reaches its stop. Hold until rotation stops, neutralize rudder, recover from the dive smoothly. Practice spins should be planned to finish recovery at least 4000 ft AGL.
keyFacts: Carb heat, primer locked, fuel on, mixture rich, mags both
65 to 75 KIAS, flaps up, level landing
Cycle master; if it returns, land as soon as practical
Ailerons neutral, idle, opposite rudder, forward elevator
memoryAids: Restart in order of likely cause: ICE, PRIMER, FUEL, MIXTURE, MAGS.
Engine fire: kill the fuel first. Electrical fire: kill the master first.
Glide 1.6 per thousand: double the thousands and subtract a fifth (3000 ft gives 6 minus 1.2, about 4.8 nm).
PARE for spins: Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite, Elevator forward (the POH lists ailerons first, then throttle; do both together before the rudder).
traps: Turning back to the runway after a low altitude engine failure.
Slowing below 60 KIAS to stretch a glide.
Extending flaps on an iced up airplane.
Resetting a popped breaker after an electrical fire.
Using the engine fire checklist for an electrical fire, or the reverse.

title: 152 Performance and Loading
summary: How to read the 152 takeoff, landing and cruise tables and run a weight and balance in five minutes.
html:
Numbers here come from the 1978 Model 152 POH. Other model years and printings differ in a few places. The POH and the weight and balance sheet kept in the club airplane are the documents that govern; check them before you fly.

Reading the takeoff and landing tables

Both Section 5 tables assume 1670 lb, short field technique, a paved, level, dry runway and zero wind. Takeoff is flaps 10 with full throttle before brake release, lift off at 50 and 54 KIAS at 50 ft. Landing is flaps 30, power off, maximum braking and 54 KIAS at 50 ft. Columns are 0 to 40 degrees C in 10 degree steps; rows are sea level to 8000 ft pressure altitude in 1000 ft steps.

The POH suggests a conservative shortcut: read the next higher altitude and the next higher temperature instead of interpolating.

CorrectionTakeoffLanding
HeadwindMinus 10 percent per 9 knotsMinus 10 percent per 9 knots
Tailwind (up to 10 knots)Plus 10 percent per 2 knotsPlus 10 percent per 2 knots
Dry grassAdd 15 percent of the ground rollAdd 45 percent of the ground roll

The grass penalty is added to both the ground roll and the total distance, since the extra distance is all on the ground.

Worked takeoff

Field at 2500 ft pressure altitude, 15 degrees C, 6 knot headwind, paved. Read 3000 ft and 20 degrees C: ground roll 1000 ft, total over 50 ft 1870 ft. Wind: 6 divided by 9 is about two thirds of a step, about 7 percent off. Result: ground roll about 930 ft, total about 1740 ft.

Worked landing

Same field, dry grass, calm wind. Read 3000 ft and 20 degrees C: ground roll 540 ft, total 1305 ft. Grass adds 45 percent of 540, about 245 ft. Result: ground roll about 785 ft, total about 1550 ft.

Sample rows to recognize

Pressure alt, tempTakeoff roll / totalLanding roll / total
Sea level, 20 C755 / 1390485 / 1215
2000 ft, 30 C980 / 1820535 / 1300
4000 ft, 20 C1100 / 2080560 / 1335
6000 ft, 30 C1455 / 2855625 / 1440
8000 ft, 40 C1940 / 4195695 / 1555

Takeoff distance more than triples from a cool sea level day to a hot 8000 ft day, while landing distance grows far less. Density altitude hurts takeoff the most.

Climb

Rate of climb at 1670 lb and full throttle runs from about 715 fpm at sea level on a standard day down to about 300 fpm at 10,000 ft. The time, fuel and distance to climb table runs from sea level; to climb from one altitude to another, subtract the two rows. Add 0.8 gallon for start, taxi and takeoff, and add 10 percent to time, fuel and distance for each 10 degrees C above standard.

Cruise and fuel

6000 ft, standard tempPowerKTASGPH
2500 RPM75%1056.1
2400 RPM67%1005.4
2300 RPM60%954.9
2200 RPM54%894.4

The cruise speeds assume wheel fairings, worth about 2 knots. Fuel flows assume the POH lean setting; the POH warns that technique and conditions can change range and endurance by 10 percent or more. The range and endurance charts already hold back a 45 minute reserve at 45 percent power (2.8 gallons).

Worked endurance

22 gallons left at cruise, 4.9 GPH: 22 divided by 4.9 is about 4.5 hours dry tanks. Day VFR reserve is 30 minutes (14 CFR 91.151), so plan no more than about 4.0 hours; at night the reserve is 45 minutes, leaving about 3.7 hours. A club rule of one hour reserve is common and smart in a 24.5 gallon airplane.

Weight and balance

Start with the basic empty weight and moment from the airplane's own sheet (it includes unusable fuel and full oil). Add each item with the Loading Graph, or with weight times arm divided by 1000. Plot total weight against total moment/1000 on the CG moment envelope, or divide moment by weight and compare with the CG limits.

Baggage area 284

CG is 54,400 divided by 1627, about 33.4 in. At 1627 lb the forward limit is about 32.4 in (31.0 plus 277/320 of 1.65) and the aft limit is 36.5, so this loading is fine. Two adults and full fuel very often run into the 1670 lb limit in a 152; then fuel is what you trade. Every 6 lb over is one gallon left behind.

Fuel sits aft of a typical loaded CG, so burning it moves the CG forward a little. In the example, landing with 4 gallons left moves the CG about 0.7 in forward; check the landing CG too when a loading starts near the forward limit.

Using the 15 percent takeoff grass factor on landing.

Forgetting the 0.8 gallon taxi allowance or the required reserve in fuel planning.

title: University Airport, Davis (KEDU)
summary: Your home field: the numbers, the pattern, the neighbors and what to watch for on every departure.
html:
The field

University Airport is a nontowered field owned by UC Davis, about 1 mile southwest of campus. It has a single asphalt runway, 17/35, 3,176 by 60 feet, at about 70 feet MSL. The old identifier 2Q3 has been replaced by KEDU, so use KEDU when you file, search weather or look it up in the Chart Supplement.

ItemKEDU
Runway17/35, 3,176 x 60 ft, asphalt
Elevationabout 70 ft MSL
PatternLeft traffic both runways, about 870 ft MSL (800 AGL)
CTAF and UNICOM123.075
WeatherAWOS 3 on 119.025
Fuel100LL self serve, 24 hours
TowerNone. Self announce on CTAF

Things that bite here

  • Trees near both ends. Trees up to about 65 ft stand south of the creek off the Runway 35 end, and trees about 40 ft tall sit on the west side near the Runway 17 threshold. Fly a stabilized approach and do not drag it in low.
  • Noise sensitive area to the north. Follow the published noise abatement procedure and avoid low passes over town.
  • Model aircraft. A remote control field operates about 5 nm northeast, surface to 1,200 AGL, sunrise to sunset.
  • Busy neighbor. Yolo County (KDWA) is only about 4 nm away with its own pattern and CTAF 123.0. Listen to both frequencies on the way in and out.

Valley weather

  • Summer heat and density altitude. A 100 F afternoon at sea level gives a density altitude near 2,700 ft. The 152 climbs noticeably worse; run the POH takeoff numbers.
  • Delta breeze. Afternoon southwest winds off the Delta are common in warm months and can bring a crosswind and gusts on Runway 17.
  • Tule fog. In late fall and winter, calm clear nights after rain produce dense radiation fog in the valley that can sit until midday.
  • Smoke. Wildfire smoke in summer and fall can drop visibility to marginal VFR or worse. Check the METARs and visibility forecasts, not just the sky.
keyFacts: about 870 ft MSL, left traffic both runways
memoryAids: One two three, oh seven five: KEDU CTAF 123.075.
traps: Using 122.8 or the old identifier 2Q3 from older notes.
Forgetting the trees on short final to Runway 35.
Treating a hot afternoon like a standard day: run density altitude every summer flight.

title: The Neighborhood: Airspace and First Cross Countries
summary: Who controls the airspace around Davis, where the towered fields are, and sensible first trips.
html:
Airspace around Davis

Always confirm on the current San Francisco sectional and the Chart Supplement. The big picture:

AirportDistanceWhat it means for you
Sacramento International (SMF)about 14 nmClass C. Establish two way radio contact with approach before entering. Mode C and ADS-B Out required in and above it.
Sacramento Executive (SAC)about 14 nmClass D, tower 0600 to 2100, tower 119.5, ATIS 118.075. A good place for the three solo full stop landings at a towered airport.
McClellan (MCC) and Mather (MHR)about 20 nm and moreTowered fields east of Sacramento. Check tower hours before planning a landing.
Beale AFBto the northMilitary airspace with restricted areas nearby. Check the chart, NOTAMs and TFRs before any flight north.
Yolo County (KDWA)about 4 nmNontowered, 6,000 ft runway, right traffic Runway 16, left traffic Runway 34.
Nut Tree (VCB)about 12 nmNontowered, Vacaville.

Practice areas

The flat farmland north and west of Davis is good for ground reference maneuvers: straight roads and field boundaries make rectangular courses and S turns easy to set up. West toward Winters and Lake Berryessa the terrain rises into the Coast Range, so mind your altitude and glide options there. Agree on the area and altitudes with your CFI and the club.

First cross countries

  • Sutter County (O52). Flat, simple, a classic first trip.
  • Placerville (PVF). Introduces rising terrain and a hilltop field: great for density altitude and approach planning.
  • Ukiah (UKI). Longer, over the Coast Range, more planning.

For each route: check airspace along the line, especially the SMF Class C shelves, pick checkpoints every 10 to 15 nm, choose a diversion airport, and get a full briefing.
keyFacts: Beale AFB military and restricted airspace
traps: Calling Sacramento Executive a Class C: it is Class D. SMF is the Class C.
Planning a towered landing outside tower hours.
